articles.title: Operationalizing ICH E17 in Multiregional Clinical Trials: A Practical Roadmap for AI-Enabled and Quantitative Methods as Enabling Tools.
articles.abstract: ICH E17 harmonized the design and interpretation of multiregional clinical trials (MRCTs), yet almost a decade after adoption, its operationalization remains inconsistent across several areas: regional definition, assessment of regional heterogeneity, evaluation of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, pooling, bridging and extrapolation, and integration of real-world data. This White Paper offers a practical roadmap for operationalizing ICH E17 across the MRCT lifecycle (planning, conduct, and submission) in which artificial intelligence (AI), pharmacometric, and biostatistical methods are treated as enabling tools rather than as the primary subject. In this paper, for each decision point, we frame a context of use, decision consequence, validation expectation, bias assessment, documentation need, and likely regulatory engagement pathway, and we distinguish approaches that are usable today for operational support from those that may provide supportive evidence with appropriate validation and those that remain exploratory. We do not propose specific regulatory recommendations; rather, we intend this roadmap to stimulate cross-stakeholder discussion and the accumulation of shared, well-documented use cases that could, in time, inform future implementation-oriented guidance.

articles.title: The Pharmacological Basis of SGLT2 Inhibitor-Mediated Kidney Protection: From Proximal Tubular Mechanisms to Clinical Outcomes.
articles.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) worldwide despite advances in glycemic control, blood pressure management, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade. The introduction of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors has fundamentally changed the management of CKD by consistently reducing kidney disease progression and cardiovascular events in patients both with and without diabetes. These findings indicate that the benefits of SGLT2 inhibition extend beyond glucose lowering and reflect broader effects on cardiorenal physiology. This review examines the pharmacological mechanisms underlying SGLT2 inhibitor-mediated kidney protection, integrating experimental evidence with findings from major clinical outcome trials. Current evidence supports a hierarchical mechanistic model in which inhibition of proximal tubular sodium-glucose reabsorption represents the primary pharmacological event, restoring tubule-glomerular feedback, reducing intraglomerular pressure, and lowering tubular transport workload. These upstream hemodynamic and metabolic effects are thought to initiate downstream improvements in kidney oxygen balance, mitochondrial function, inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis, although the relative contribution of these pathways remains incompletely defined. We further examine how contemporary clinical trials validate this mechanistic framework across diverse CKD populations, including patients with and without diabetes and across a broad range of kidney function and albuminuria. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for phenotype-specific treatment strategies, rational combination therapy with complementary kidney-protective agents, and future directions in biomarker-guided precision medicine. Collectively, current evidence supports SGLT2 inhibitors as integrated cardiorenal therapies that modify fundamental determinants of CKD progression and provide the pharmacological foundation of contemporary kidney-protective treatment.

articles.title: Structural characterisation of the effect of 5-chloroindole on orthosteric activation of murine 5-HT3A receptors.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: 5-HT3 receptors play a central role in gut-brain signalling, and their hyperactivity is associated with pathologies ranging from chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting to irritable bowel syndrome. While the principles governing 5-HT3R orthosteric pharmacology are well established (spanning antagonists, partial agonists and full agonists), structural insights into allosteric mechanisms remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the mechanisms by which a positive modulator of 5-HT3R, 5-chloroindole, potentiates agonist response by fine-tuning orthosteric activation of this receptor. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Here, we investigated the molecular basis of modulation by 5-chloroindole (5-CI), a selective positive allosteric modulator, using cryo-EM and electrophysiology. We present 5-HT3AR structures in the presence of 5-CI alone, as well as in combination with either submaximal concentrations of 5-HT or saturating concentrations of the partial agonist SMP-100. KEY RESULTS: Our results reveal that 5-CI potentiates 5-HT3R through a distinct mechanism involving co-occupancy of the orthosteric site and with additional modulation through an intersubunit site in the transmembrane domain. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: This mode of action is reminiscent of benzodiazepine modulation in GABAARs, yet it notably occurs within homomeric binding sites. Together, these findings establish the structural basis for the previously reported ago-allosteric mechanism of 5-CI, which becomes functionally apparent only in the presence of agonistic ligands.

articles.title: Glucocorticoid receptor dimerisation controls inflammation and tumour progression in colorectal cancer via a highly specific immune gene network.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The progression of ulcerative colitis (UC) to colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a major clinical challenge. Glucocorticoids (GCs) are widely used for the treatment of UC and also are included in therapeutic regimens for CRC. The transcriptional mechanisms through which GCs regulate inflammation and tumourigenesis via the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) remain incompletely understood. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: GRdim mice, expressing a dimerisation-defective GR with predominantly monomeric activity, were subjected to the azoxymethane/dextran sodium sulphate model of colitis-associated CRC. Inflammation, tumour development and survival were assessed and complemented by transcriptomic profiling, network analysis, tumour organoid experiments and cross-species comparisons. KEY RESULTS: Impaired GR dimerisation attenuated colon inflammation, as reflected by improved epithelial barrier integrity and reduced expression of pro-inflammatory genes. Tumourigenesis followed a biphasic pattern, with delayed tumour onset but accelerated tumour growth at later stages. Transcriptomic analyses revealed a distinct inflammatory signature in GRdim tumours, characterised by altered immune-related pathways and reduced gene expression linked to myeloid cell recruitment and activation. Integration with scRNA-seq datasets and tumour organoid studies indicated that altered GR activity affects both tumour cells and the tumour microenvironment. Cross-species analyses revealed an overlap between the gene signature distinguishing GRwt and GRdim murine tumours and gene expression patterns in human CRC that are associated with poor survival. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: GR dimerisation differentially contributes to the anti-inflammatory and tumour-related GC effects, thereby uncoupling the control of colitis from the regulation of tumour progression, highlighting potential limitations of selectively targeting GR monomer activity in therapeutic regimens.

articles.title: Beyond antigens: TLR9-β-glucan nanocomplexes for 'X' respiratory viral infections.
articles.abstract: Pathogen-specific vaccines provide durable immunity, but the delayed rollout during emerging viral outbreaks leaves populations vulnerable. Tobuse et al. address this gap, demonstrating that intranasal administration of K3-SPG, an antigen-free, water-soluble β-glucan/Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9)-agonist nanocomplex induces biphasic, tissue-restricted innate memory, conferring broad, antigen-independent protection against diverse respiratory viruses by limiting lung pathology.

articles.title: Characterization of endocytosis and intracellular signalling of the gastrin-releasing peptide receptor in pruritus.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Chronic pruritus (itch) is a widespread issue affecting one in four adults, with unmet needs for effective treatment. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are central to itch signalling and represent a major therapeutic target. Endosomal GPCR signalling introduces new avenues for understanding how GPCR activity is regulated and how it contributes to disease states like chronic pruritus. The gastrin-releasing peptide receptor (GRPR) is a key mediator of pruritus in the spinal cord, but the regulation of GRPR signalling and the role of endosomal GRPR in itch sensation remain poorly understood. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: We investigated GRPR internalization and intracellular trafficking in pruritus. Agonist-induced GRPR internalization and trafficking were quantified using bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) and microscopy. Endosome-mediated ERK signalling was measured using compartmentalized fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) biosensors, and G protein recruitment to endosomes was assessed via NanoBit BRET and GEMTA assays. To block endosomal signalling, we utilized pH-sensitive mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) that accumulate in endosomes to deliver RC-3095, a GRPR-specific antagonist, intracellularly. KEY RESULTS: These studies show that GRPR can recruit and activate G proteins from the endosomal compartment in HEK cells, and targeting endosomal GRPR signalling using pH-sensitive MSN-RC-3095 nanoparticles can block scratching behaviour in mice. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: Our results demonstrate a role for GRPR endocytosis, trafficking and signalling in the transmission of itch sensation. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of using intracellularly targeted antagonists to inhibit GRPR signalling, thereby providing a novel strategy for developing therapeutics to block GRPR-mediated pruritus.

articles.title: A Transgenic Pig Model for human Metabolic Disorders Defines the relationship between the colon pathological phenotype of metabolic disease, the microbiota and the intestinal barrier.
articles.abstract: Metabolic disorders are increasingly associated with intestinal dysfunction and colorectal diseases, yet the pathological characteristics and underlying mechanisms of intestinal injury under metabolic stress remain poorly understood. Here, we established a transgenic (TG) Bama pig model by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of three humanized susceptibility genes and subjected the pigs to a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFHSD) for 4, 8, or 12 months to investigate metabolic disorder-associated colonic dysfunction. HFHSD intervention induced marked alterations in serum biochemical parameters and disrupted colonic mucosal architecture, characterized by glandular disorganization and crypt distortion. Colonic tissues from TG pigs exhibited reduced populations of goblet cells, CD8⁺ T cells, and CD79A⁺ B cells, accompanied by pronounced activation of mitophagy, indicating impaired epithelial barrier integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. In parallel, microbial diversity and IgA levels were reduced in the colonic contents of TG pigs, accompanied by an increased abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria, particularly Escherichia-Shigella. Metabolomic profiling of colonic contents further revealed significant alterations in the intestinal metabolic landscape, including decreased levels of isobutyric acid and isovaleric acid and an increased level of myristic acid, a metabolite associated with autophagy-related processes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that metabolic disorders are associated with coordinated alterations in colonic mucosal integrity, mucosal immunity, mitochondrial quality control, gut microbiota, and intestinal metabolism. The humanized TG Bama pig model provides a clinically relevant large-animal platform for investigating the pathophysiology of metabolic disorder-associated colonic diseases and may facilitate the development and preclinical evaluation of therapeutic strategies targeting intestinal dysfunction.

articles.title: Targeting Proviral CNOT1 with Mogroside V Restores MARCH8-Mediated Ubiquitination of M2 and Blocks Influenza Infection.
Chronic hypoxia drives coronary artery pathology via TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ influx and phase separation-dependent cGAS-STING activation.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is frequently complicated by coronary artery remodeling and dysfunction, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. This study investigated whether and how chronic hypoxia drives coronary artery dysfunction through TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ influx and cGAS-STING activation in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). METHODS AND RESULTS: A rat model of PH was established by exposure to chronic hypoxia. Coronary artery structure and function were assessed by histology and wire myography. In vitro experiments were performed using cultured SMCs, with molecular and cellular analyses including qPCR, western blotting, immunofluorescence, live-cell imaging, mitochondrial assays, and cell-free phase separation assays. PH rats exhibited increased coronary TRPC3/4 expression, enhanced Ca²⁺ influx, and coronary hypercontractility. In cultured SMCs, hypoxia induced mitochondrial dysfunction, mtDNA release, and cGAS condensate formation. TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ overload promoted mitochondrial damage and cGAS phase separation, while STIM1/ORAI1-mediated store-operated Ca²⁺ entry (SOCE) further contributed to STING activation. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Ca²⁺ promoted cGAS phase separation in both the presence and absence of dsDNA, and this effect was dependent on the cGAS intrinsically disordered region (IDR). Importantly, CIP3 attenuated cGAS phase separation and downstream STING signaling, thereby mitigating hypoxia-induced SMC proliferation, migration, and phenotypic switching. In PH rats, short-term treatment with VAPG-targeted CIP3 reduced right ventricular systolic pressure, attenuated pulmonary and coronary vascular remodeling, and improved coronary contractile responses. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish a novel mechanistic axis wherein chronic hypoxia drives coronary artery dysfunction via TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ influx and phase separation-dependent cGAS-STING activation. In our experimental models, targeting cGAS phase separation, particularly through IDR-directed intervention, may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for PH-associated vascular pathology.

articles.title: SPOP mutations impair CRL3SPOP-mediated survivin degradation to confer chemotherapy resistance in prostate cancer: implications for survivin-targeted therapy.
articles.abstract: Dysregulated apoptosis is a critical factor contributing to the emergence of drug resistance in cancer chemotherapy. Survivin, a key member of the inhibitor of apoptosis protein (IAP) family, is frequently overexpressed in various cancers and plays a pivotal role in apoptosis regulation. In our study, we identified CRL3SPOP as a canonical E3 ligase for survivin, mediating its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Intriguingly, prostate cancer-associated SPOP mutants lose the ability to bind survivin, thereby impairing its degradation which leads to diminished apoptosis, enhanced cell survival, and increased chemotherapy resistance in prostate cancer cells harboring SPOP mutations. Importantly, we demonstrated that depletion of survivin in SPOP-mutated cells significantly enhances apoptosis and restores chemosensitivity. This study provides a direct mechanism for the reduced level of apoptosis in prostate cancer with SPOP mutations, and demonstrated that survivin might be a therapeutic target for SPOP-mutated patients and provided new strategies to overcome chemotherapy resistance.

articles.title: Bioengineering enucleated cancer cells infected with oncolytic viruses for targeted tumor metastatic immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Oncolytic virus (OV) therapy is clinically administered mainly by intratumoral injection, whereas systemic delivery remains limited by poor tumor tropism and severe side effects. Here we report a virus-concealed tumor-targeting strategy that enables systemic administration of OVs to lung metastases. We first screened and obtained the 4 T1-LUNG cell line, which exhibits high lung metastatic capacity. Enucleation was then used to treat 4 T1-LUNG cells to abolish pathogenicity while preserving other cellular characteristics. The enucleated 4 T1-LUNG cells were subsequently infected with Reovirus to form enucleated 4 T1-LUNG-Reovirus complexes (termed E4L-Rs). This delivery system increases viral payload, owing to the absence of transcriptional machinery and interferon (IFN) signaling, and protects against viral neutralization and clearance in the circulatory system. It also enables lung-specific targeting via the Cxcl12-Cxcr4 and Itgb1-Fak-Src axes, resulting in a more than 320-fold increase in viral accumulation in lung tissue. Upon reaching the lung, E4L-Rs induce immunogenic cell death (ICD) in tumor cells, promoting the expansion of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and M1 macrophages and converting immunologically 'cold' tumors into 'hot' tumors. The E4L-Rs platform thus offers a promising strategy for oncolytic virus-targeted therapy against tumor metastasis.

articles.title: mRNA-LNP vaccine encoding for Fc-scaffold antigen drives FcγR-independent immunity.
articles.abstract: While clinical translation of messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technologies has redefined vaccinology, the development of potent platforms against complex bacterial pathogens is often limited by the transient expression kinetics and rapid clearance of encoded antigens. One well established approach to enhance immunogenicity is the fusion of an Fc fragment to an antigen. However, the mechanism of Fc-mediated potentiation within mRNA-LNP systems is, yet, undefined, specifically regarding the necessity of receptor-mediated interactions. Here, we demonstrate that an mRNA-LNP vaccine, encoding an Fc-fragment fused to the Yersinia pestis F1 antigen, drives robust, protective immunity against the lethal bubonic plague by functioning as a pharmacokinetic stabilizer. Through systematic architectural design, variation of Fc isotypes, species-matched scaffolding, and glycosylation profiling, we reveal that Fc-integration extends systemic antigen bioavailability by over 300-fold, providing a sustained kinetic window for immune priming. Remarkably, immunogenicity is preserved in Fcγ receptor (FcγR)-deficient mice, as well as with a reduced FcγR-binding Fc variant, suggesting that protective immunity is independent of classical FcγR engagement in this model. These findings decouple Fc-mediated enhancement from receptor-mediated interactions, identifying structural stabilization and prolonged persistence as the primary drivers of efficacy in mRNA-LNP vaccines. Altogether, our results provide a mechanistic framework for the design of high-potency mRNA vaccines through engineered protein stability.

articles.title: GM3 lipid-coated polymeric nanoparticles for prolonged & targeted delivery of emtricitabine and tenofovir.
articles.abstract: Demanding pill adherence has made the effective use of combination oral nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) against human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) challenging. Drug-loaded implants, prodrugs, nanosuspensions, and nanoparticles of NRTIs and other compounds have been investigated to address this challenge, but improving penetration and retention in specific target tissues remains a high priority in the development of potential drug candidates. Herein, we demonstrate that the well-established NRTIs, emtricitabine (FTC) and tenofovir (TFV), can be chemically linked to poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) dendrimers to produce prodrugs and co-loaded into polymeric (poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone), PEG-PCL) nanoparticles with a lipid coating consisting of monosialodihexosylganglioside (GM3), cholesterol, and 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DPPC). The prodrugs, G2-TFV and G2.5-FTC, exhibited similar half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values (1.14 ± 0.57 μM, 0.94 ± 0.50 μM) as their free drug analogs, TFV (2.71 μM ± 1.37 μM) and FTC (0.23 ± 0.17 μM). GM3-coated nanoparticles (45-55 nm) demonstrated CD169-dependent targeting through specific binding to CD169+ myeloid cells. Importantly, a single dose of prodrug-loaded GM3 nanoparticles inhibited HIV-1 infection in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) through 28 days post-treatment, whereas inhibition by free drugs was abrogated by day 3. No cytotoxicity or inflammatory responses were observed. A single inoculation of GM3 nanoparticles in Balb/c mice showed association with myeloid cells and provided detectable levels of NRTIs in lymphoid and mucosal tissues through 42 days. Collectively, this work confirms that GM3-coated polymeric nanoparticles in combination with G2-TFV and G2.5-FTC prodrugs hold promise for overcoming PrEP barriers.

articles.title: Selective covalent targeting of thioredoxin-1 decouples bone resorption from coupling-factor signaling in osteoporosis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Excessive osteoclast-mediated bone resorption is a major pathological driver of osteoporosis. However, conventional anti-resorptive therapies may impair bone formation by disrupting osteoclast-osteoblast coupling. Natural products that suppress pathological bone resorption while preserving coupling signals may therefore offer an alternative therapeutic strategy. PURPOSE: This study aimed to identify a natural small molecule that inhibits osteoclast activity while preserving osteoclast-osteoblast coupling and to clarify its underlying molecular mechanism. METHODS: Carabrone (CB), a natural small molecule, was evaluated for its effects on osteoclast differentiation, bone resorption, apoptosis, and the expression of osteoclast-derived coupling factors. Its therapeutic efficacy was assessed in ovariectomized (OVX) osteoporosis models. Activity-based protein profiling, LC-MS/MS, mutational analysis, and biochemical and cellular assays were employed to identify and characterize the direct molecular target of CB. RESULTS: In vitro, CB markedly suppressed osteoclast differentiation and bone-resorbing activity while showing limited effects on osteoclast-derived coupling mediators, including sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), WNT10B, and CTHRC1. In vivo, CB alleviated trabecular bone loss and improved biomechanical properties. Serum OCN and P1NP levels were significantly increased relative to OVX controls. Mechanistically, CB covalently modified thioredoxin-1 (TRX1) at Cys32, Cys35, and Cys73. Mutational analyses supported a contribution of Cys73 to the cellular response to CB. CB disrupted the TRX1-NEMO interaction, inhibited NF-κB/NFATC1 signaling, and promoted osteoclast apoptosis. CONCLUSION: CB suppressed osteoclast activity while showing limited effects on measured coupling-associated mediators and osteogenic responses in vitro. These findings identify TRX1 as a pharmacologically actionable regulator of osteoclast function and establish CB as a promising lead for anti-resorptive therapies.

articles.title: Gastrodiae Rhizoma decoction ameliorates scopolamine-induced cognitive impairment by promoting hippocampal neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gastrodiae Rhizoma (GR) decoction, prepared from the dried rhizome of Gastrodia elata Blume, has been traditionally used for neurological disorders. However, its active components and mechanisms against cognitive impairment remain unclear. PURPOSE: This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of GR decoction against scopolamine-induced cognitive impairment and identified its brain-penetrating active components. METHODS: A scopolamine-induced mouse model was established, with donepezil as positive control. Cognitive function was assessed by behavioral tests. Hippocampal metabolomic profiles were analyzed. Neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity and pathway activation were evaluated by immunohistochemistry, Western blotting, Golgi staining and immunofluorescence. The chemical composition of the decoction was characterized, and its brain-penetrating components were identified. Active constituents were validated by molecular docking and in vitro experiments. RESULTS: The GR decoction significantly ameliorated cognitive impairment and restored aberrant hippocampal metabolic profiles. It activated a signaling cascade involving protein kinase A (PKA)/cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), upregulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and activating tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) in hippocampal neurons, thereby promoting neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity. TrkB inhibition partially abolished these protective effects. Gastrodin and parishin C were identified as core active components. They promoted BDNF expression via PKA/CREB pathway and the secreted BDNF activated TrkB on neural stem cells to promote proliferation. CONCLUSION: GR decoction ameliorates cognitive impairment by activating PKA/CREB/BDNF/TrkB pathway to promote hippocampal neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity. Gastrodin and parishin C are the core brain-penetrating active components responsible for these effects.

articles.title: Garlic-derived S-allyl-L-cysteine ameliorates colon-spleen axis pathology in acute colitis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: S-allyl-L-cysteine (SAC), a bioactive organosulfur compound derived from aged garlic, exhibits anti-inflammatory properties, yet its cellular targets and systemic mechanisms in ulcerative colitis (UC) remain undefined. PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate whether SAC confers protection against dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and to elucidate its mechanism of action, with a particular focus on the colon-spleen axis and neuro-immune crosstalk. METHODS: Acute colitis was induced in wild-type and CCL7 knockout mice using 2.5% DSS, followed by daily oral SAC administration (3 mg/kg). Disease severity was assessed through clinical parameters, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry. Xenium spatial transcriptomics was employed to map cellular dynamics and intercellular communication. In vitro assays using HCT116 epithelial cells, P815 mast cells, RAW264.7 macrophages, HL-60 neutrophils, and THP-1 monocytes were performed to dissect the underlying molecular mechanisms. RESULTS: SAC treatment significantly alleviated colitis symptoms, reduced mortality, preserved mucosal integrity, and decreased inflammatory cell infiltration. Spatial transcriptomics revealed that injured epithelial cells released TNF-α, which activated subepithelial mast cells via NFκB2 nuclear translocation to produce CCL7. SAC was preferentially and efficiently internalized by mast cells, not macrophages, to suppress this TNF-α/NFκB2/CCL7 signaling pathway. This inhibition abrogated splenic myeloid recruitment through CCR1/2 and CXCR2, supporting a colon-spleen axis that orchestrates systemic inflammation. SAC also redirected neuronal transcription toward repair-oriented pathways and upregulated FTH1, redistributing iron from pro-inflammatory macrophages to epithelial cells. CCL7 deficiency phenocopied SAC's protective effects, with attenuated neuronal-adjacent neutrophilia and preserved mucosal integrity. CONCLUSION: We unveil an epithelial-TNF-α-mast cell-CCL7-spleen-neuronal injury axis as a key contribution of colitis propagation and suggest SAC as a dietary agent that concurrently curbs systemic myeloid recruitment and relieves enteric neuronal inflammation, thereby attenuating colitis-associated abdominal pain.

articles.title: Luteoloside from Crataegus pinnatifida Bunge alleviates metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis by restoring mitochondrial homeostasis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a progressive liver disease driven by lipid overload, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation, yet effective pharmacological therapies remain limited. The leaves of Crataegus pinnatifida Bunge (Hawthorn) have long been used for metabolic disorders, but its principal anti-MASH constituent and underlying mechanism remain unclear. METHODS: A flavonoid-rich hawthorn leaf extract (HLE) was optimally prepared and initially evaluated in free fatty acid-induced HepG2 cells. Integrated transcriptomic and network pharmacology analyses were performed to prioritize candidate targets and signaling pathways. Phytochemical profiling, affinity ultrafiltration screening, and molecular docking were used to identify the principal bioactive constituent of HLE. The efficacy and mechanism of the identified compound were further validated in FFA-induced cells and high-fat/high-cholesterol-fed rats. RESULTS: Flavonoid-rich HLE markedly attenuated free fatty acid-induced lipotoxicity, as evidenced by reduced lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cytokine expression. Integrated transcriptomic and network analyses prioritized the AMP-activated catalytic subunit alpha 1 (PRKAA1)/AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) axis as a central target. Among compounds identified in HLE, the flavone glucoside luteoloside emerged as the leading AMPKα-targeting candidate based on affinity ultrafiltration and molecular docking analyses. In vitro and in vivo, luteoloside alleviated metabolic dysfunction, hepatic steatosis, oxidative stress, inflammation, and steatohepatitic injury. Mechanistically, luteoloside restored AMPKα phosphorylation and promoted peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α)-dependent mitochondrial reprogramming, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid β-oxidation, and antioxidant defense. Importantly, PRKAA1 silencing markedly blunted these protective effects, establishing AMPKα as a required mediator. Integrated hepatic transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses further supported AMPK-driven mitochondrial reprogramming as a core mechanism underlying luteoloside action. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies the flavone glucoside luteoloside as a principal anti-MASH component from hawthorn leaf and demonstrates that its therapeutic effects are mediated through AMPKα-dependent restoration of mitochondrial homeostasis. By activating the AMPKα-PGC-1α axis, luteoloside improves mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative metabolism, and redox balance, thereby alleviating lipotoxicity and steatohepatitic injury. These findings provide both a chemical basis and a mechanistic rationale for the development of hawthorn leaf-derived interventions for MASH.

articles.title: Protective effects and underlying mechanisms of naringenin in myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury: a systematic review and preclinical meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (MI/RI) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality. Current interventions have limited efficacy and significant adverse effects, creating an urgent need for safer alternatives. Naringenin, a natural flavonoid with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties, has shown promising cardioprotective potential in preclinical studies. However, the evidence remains fragmented, and no systematic quantitative evaluation has been performed. METHODS: We searched five databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI) from inception to January 2025 for preclinical animal studies on naringenin in MI/RI. Primary outcome measures included myocardial infarction area, myocardial enzyme levels, and cardiac function-related indicators. Apoptosis, inflammatory factors, and oxidative stress-related indicators were defined as secondary outcome measures. Statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.6.1. The standardized mean difference, adjusted for small sample sizes using Hedges' g, along with the corresponding 95% confidence interval was used as the effect size measure. Heterogeneity among studies was evaluated using I2. The analysis used restricted maximum likelihood as the random-effects estimator, and the Hartung-Knapp correction was applied to ensure an accurate confidence interval. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the SYRCLE risk of bias tool for animal studies. A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was conducted to investigate the impact of studies with extreme effect sizes on the pooled results. Subgroup analyses were conducted to identify heterogeneity sources. Funnel plots were used to qualitatively assess publication bias. Egger's test, combined with the trim-and-fill method, was further applied for quantitative correction based on qualitative funnel plot inspection when necessary. RESULTS: A total of 32 studies involving 544 experimental animals were analyzed. The findings from the meta-analysis indicated that naringenin intervention significantly reduced the area of myocardial infarction (Hedges' g = -3.75), as well as lowered levels of myocardial enzymes (lactate dehydrogenase, LDH: Hedges' g = -6.10; creatine kinase myocardial band, CK-MB: Hedges' g = -6.79) and decreased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (Hedges' g = -3.57). Furthermore, naringenin significantly improved various cardiac function indices, including the maximum rate of left ventricular pressure decrease (-LVdP/dtmax: Hedges' g = 4.45), the maximum rate of left ventricular pressure increase (+LVdP/dtmax: Hedges' g = 3.31), and left ventricular developed pressure (LVDP: Hedges' g = 3.80) (all P < 0.05). Although there was a downward trend in CK levels, this difference did not reach statistical significance (Hedges' g = -7.77, 95% CI [-15.79, 0.25], P = 0.056). Naringenin significantly increased Bcl-2 protein expression (Hedges' g = 6.14) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity (Hedges' g = 6.26). Additionally, it significantly reduced the apoptosis index (Hedges' g = -4.64), Bax protein expression (Hedges' g = -3.64), interleukin-1β (IL-1β) levels (Hedges' g = -4.93), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels (Hedges' g = -3.57), and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels (Hedges' g = -5.05) (all P < 0.05). Although there was an upward trend in heart rate, this difference was not statistically significant (Hedges' g = 1.22, 95% CI [-0.29, 2.74], P = 0.098). CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis presents robust evidence indicating that naringenin possesses cardioprotective properties against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (MI/RI). The mechanism of action appears to involve the attenuation of oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis, along with improvement of cardiac function. The conclusions drawn from this analysis must be approached with caution due to methodological limitations and potential publication bias. Further rigorous preclinical and clinical trials are warranted to fully establish its translational potential. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2026.3.0057 identifier, INPLASY202630057.

articles.title: Effect of compound kushen injection on immune function in patients with lung cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lung cancer remains a major global public health burden, characterized by high morbidity and mortality. The tumor immune microenvironment of lung cancer displays complex and dynamically changing immune landscapes, where diverse cell types collectively construct an immunosuppressive tumor ecosystem. Accordingly, boosting host immune function represents a promising therapeutic strategy to improve clinical outcomes and alleviate treatment-related adverse reactions in patients with lung cancer. OBJECTIVE: To systematically analyze the effects, efficacy, and safety of Compound Kushen Injection (CKI) combined with conventional treatment on improving immune function in lung cancer patients, providing evidence-based medical evidence for clinical practice. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in major Chinese and English databases from their inception to 25 March 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the impact of CKI on immune function in lung cancer patients were included. Quality assessment and data extraction were performed, and statistical analyses were conducted using Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 18.0 software. RESULTS: A total of 3846 patients from 39 RCTs were included (1971 in the experimental group and 1875 in the control group). Compared with conventional treatment alone, CKI combined with conventional treatment significantly enhanced immune function, as evidenced by increased levels of CD3+, CD4+, CD4+/CD8+ ratio, and natural killer (NK) cells, and decreased levels of CD8+ cells. Additionally, this combination improved the objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR), reduced carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels, improved Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) scores, prolonged 1-year overall survival, and effectively reduced treatment-related adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal reactions, myelosuppression, hepatorenal toxicity, and fatigue. CONCLUSION: Current evidence indicates that CKI combined with conventional treatment provides multiple clinical benefits for lung cancer patients. However, the limited available evidence may compromise the reliability of our conclusions. Rigorously designed multicenter double-blind randomized controlled trials with staged analyses and long-term follow-up are needed to validate these findings. All findings should be interpreted as exploratory. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261384207, identifier CRD420261384207.

articles.title: Short-term efficacy and safety of guselkumab for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis: a systematic review and meta-analysis with a pasi response-depth analysis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the short-term efficacy and safety of guselkumab in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and to explore whether its comparative advantage over adalimumab changes across increasingly stringent PASI response thresholds. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data were systematically searched from inception to April 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating guselkumab in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. Two reviewers independently screened the literature, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.3. All efficacy and safety data were extracted at Week 16. In a post hoc exploratory response-depth analysis of the three head-to-head trials, the relative treatment effect of guselkumab versus adalimumab was examined across PASI75, PASI90, and PASI100 thresholds. RESULTS: Six RCTs comprising 997 patients in the guselkumab group, 625 in the adalimumab group, and 548 in the placebo group were included. At Week 16, guselkumab was associated with a significantly higher PASI90 response rate than adalimumab (RR = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.35-1.62, P < 0.001) and placebo (RR = 28.29, 95% CI: 16.69-47.96, P < 0.001). The exploratory head-to-head response-depth analysis showed a progressive increase in the relative advantage of guselkumab as the PASI target became more stringent: RR = 1.25 (95% CI: 1.18-1.32) for PASI75, 1.48 (1.35-1.62) for PASI90, and 1.85 (1.54-2.23) for PASI100. Corresponding crude response proportions across the three direct-comparison trials were 87.8% versus 71.0%, 70.8% versus 48.2%, and 35.3% versus 19.0%, respectively. Most short-term safety comparisons were imprecise and did not reach statistical significance. For upper respiratory tract infection versus adalimumab, the pooled estimate was RR = 1.69 (95% CI: 0.99-2.87; P = 0.05) based on two trials; the confidence interval only narrowly included the null and the comparison was underpowered. CONCLUSION: Beyond confirming greater Week 16 efficacy of guselkumab, this meta-analysis suggests that its relative advantage over adalimumab becomes more pronounced as the treatment target shifts from PASI75 toward near-complete or complete skin clearance. This response-depth pattern may be clinically relevant in an era in which PASI90 and PASI100 are increasingly used as treatment goals. Most evaluated short-term safety outcomes did not show statistically significant differences; however, estimates were imprecise and should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence.

articles.title: Teacher training for the school-based prevention of alcohol and other drug use: a scoping review with implications for pharmaceutical sciences.
articles.abstract: Teacher training is integral to school-based prevention of alcohol and other psychoactive substance use, yet its content, implementation, and evaluation are reported unevenly. To map school-based prevention initiatives incorporating teacher training and examine their structure, evaluation, and documented pharmacological and toxicological content. This scoping review followed JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR. PubMed/MEDLINE, ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and LILACS/BVS were searched without formal publication-date or language restrictions. Multiple reports on the same initiative were linked for initiative-level synthesis. The review included 198 reports representing 142 initiatives, of which 138 underwent cross-cutting coding. Teacher training differed in delivery, duration, implementation support, and evaluation. Among the 138 initiatives, 108 (78.3%) documented some form of program evaluation, but only 13 (9.4%) reported independent or external evaluation. Teacher-training outcomes were reported in 72 initiatives (52.2%), and student outcomes in 73 (52.9%); these indicators did not establish effectiveness attributable to training. Specific toxicological content was documented in 22 initiatives (15.9%), broad or nonspecific mentions in 30 (21.7%), and insufficient information to determine its presence in 86 (62.3%). Risk communication was documented in 62 initiatives (44.9%). Teacher training was embedded in heterogeneous school-based prevention programs, with uneven implementation support and evaluation. Limited reporting of scientific content does not demonstrate its absence from training. Clearer descriptions of curricula and implementation conditions, together with evaluations distinguishing teacher learning, classroom practice, and student outcomes, are needed. Collaboration between Pharmaceutical Sciences and education may support evidence-informed, age-appropriate, and non-stigmatizing prevention content.

articles.title: Catheter tip placement for intrathecal therapy in refractory cancer pain: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intrathecal drug delivery (IDD) provides continuous administration of analgesics into the intrathecal space. Although catheter tip placement is considered important for treatment success, evidence of its impact on long-term clinical outcomes remains limited, particularly when considering pain distribution, cancer type, and the intrathecal medication used. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the evidence of catheter tip positioning in patients with refractory cancer pain. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EMBASE were systematically searched from inception to October 2025. Studies including patients with refractory cancer pain treated with implanted IDD were included. Study quality was assessed using a modified Downs and Black checklist. Meta-regression was performed to evaluate associations between treatment success and catheter tip location, pain distribution, and intrathecal medication type. RESULTS: Of 8,414 identified articles, 23 studies were included (14 in meta-analysis). Catheter tip placement descriptively corresponded to cancer type and pain location. However, meta-regression analyses showed no significant association between treatment success and catheter tip location (p = 0.914), pain location (p = 0.407), or intrathecal medication category (p = 0.937). CONCLUSIONS: Descriptive findings support anatomically guided catheter placement, but the available evidence is insufficient to determine whether catheter tip location or other examined factors are associated with treatment success. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251150374 identifier is CRD420251150374.

articles.title: Inhaled biologics: A paradigm shift in drug delivery for proteins, vaccines, and gene-based therapeutics.
articles.abstract: Pulmonary drug delivery has emerged as a promising platform for the administration of biologics, offering direct access to the respiratory tract while minimising systemic exposure and associated adverse effects. Recent advances in inhalation technologies, formulation engineering, and carrier systems have significantly expanded the scope of inhaled biologics beyond conventional therapies. This review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging inhaled biologics, including proteins, peptides, monoclonal antibodies, gene therapies, mRNA therapeutics, siRNA, CRISPR-based systems, vaccines, and nanocarrier-enabled delivery platforms. Key physiological barriers to pulmonary delivery, such as mucociliary clearance, alveolar macrophage uptake, mucus penetration, and epithelial transport, are critically discussed along with contemporary strategies to overcome these challenges. Recent developments in lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, liposomes, exosomes, and inhalable dry powder systems are highlighted for their role in enhancing stability, targeting efficiency, and therapeutic outcomes. The review also examines clinical translation, regulatory considerations, aerosol performance, pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic relationships, and the integration of artificial intelligence in formulation design and precision delivery. Marketed inhaled biologics remain limited to a few products, including inhaled insulin. In contrast, most inhaled monoclonal antibodies, gene-based therapies, gene-editing approaches, and pulmonary vaccine platforms remain investigational, with evidence derived primarily from clinical studies at different stages or from preclinical models. This review distinguishes marketed products from clinical-stage candidates and preclinical proof-of-concept studies to clarify the current state of pulmonary biologic delivery.

articles.title: Three-fluid nozzle spray drying as a pharmaceutical particle engineering approach: A review.
articles.abstract: Three-fluid nozzle (3-FN) spray drying has emerged as a versatile particle-engineering approach that atomizes two liquid feeds through separate channels which meet only at droplet formation. Unlike conventional two-fluid nozzle (2-FN) spray drying, 3-FN allows components with different solvent requirements, incompatibilities or intended spatial distributions to be processed in a single step. This review evaluates 3-FN spray drying as a distinct pharmaceutical technology rather than an extension of conventional spray drying. It first examines how the spray-drying process determines particle structure. Factors such as nozzle design, how the two feeds mix, their relative flow rates and their physical properties determine where each component ends up as the droplet dries. This can produce particles with separate core and shell regions, a gradual change in composition from the centre to the surface, or components mixed throughout the particle. It then reviews how the technology has been used for different pharmaceutical applications, including improving drug solubility, controlling drug release, encapsulating materials and producing inhaled formulations, amorphous systems and co-crystals. It also examines studies that directly compare two-fluid and three-fluid nozzles to determine when using a three-fluid nozzle provides a meaningful advantage. The evidence indicates that 3-FN is most useful where spatial separation, core-shell structuring, surface modification or processing of incompatible solvent systems is required, but does not consistently outperform 2-FN for homogeneous formulations and remains constrained by yield, scale-up, reproducibility and long-term stability. A decision framework guides nozzle selection, and priorities are identified in mechanistic modeling of in-nozzle mixing, standardized head-to-head comparisons, and ICH-compliant stability and scale-up studies.

articles.title: Spatial pharmacology of breast cancer immune Evasion: Omics-Guided drug target discovery and therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Breast cancer exhibits profound spatial heterogeneity in immune evasion, with conventional bulk omics unable to resolve intratumoral immunosuppressive gradients that drive variable drug response and therapeutic resistance. Existing reviews largely focus on spatial omics technologies or tumor immunology and lack a pharmacological framework for understanding how spatial architecture shapes drug-target accessibility, intratumoral drug exposure, and zone-specific resistance. Building on the emerging concept of spatial pharmacology, this review extends its application by integrating tumor spatial microenvironment structure, spatial cell-cell interactions, spatial multiomics mapping, and regional drug distribution to address spatial heterogeneity-mediated drug sensitivity and resistance. We describe subtype-specific spatial immune evasion features, spatial omics technologies, and spatial pharmacology in breast cancer - including spatial profiling of drug distribution, omics-driven target discovery, druggability evaluation, and the corresponding resistance mechanisms and therapeutic strategies. Current limitations include technical bottlenecks in spatial resolution, insufficient druggability validation of spatial targets, and translational gaps between spatial discovery and clinical drug development. In the future, spatial pharmacology will provide guidance for the stratification of precision immunotherapy and accelerate the development of spatially informed drug therapies for breast cancer.

articles.title: CFTR regulation of ROS-mediated cellular injury and immune dysregulation in cystic fibrosis.
articles.abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a life-limiting autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, most commonly F508del. Mutant CFTR disrupts transepithelial ion transport and intracellular redox homeostasis, leading to excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Evidence from cohort studies, human airway organoid models, and single-cell transcriptomic analyses published between 2020 and 2026 has prompted substantial revision of the prevailing linear model of CF pathogenesis. These studies demonstrate that misfolded CFTR can independently initiate oxidative stress and low-grade inflammation in the absence of microbial colonization. Mitochondrial ROS (mitoROS) constitute a central signaling hub linking F508del-induced protein misfolding to transcriptional suppression of the Nrf2 antioxidant program, constitutive activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, and dysregulation of TLR-cytokine cascades. Triple CFTR modulator regimens, including elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) and the once-daily combination vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor (Alyftrek, FDA-approved December 2024 for patients ≥6 years carrying at least one F508del or other Alyftrek-responsive CFTR variant; pivotal SKYLINE 102/103 trials demonstrated non-inferiority versus ETI in largely ETI-eligible populations), have transformed clinical care. However, multi-omics data indicate that these agents do not fully restore airway redox homeostasis or resolve persistent low-grade inflammation, even when CFTR channel activity recovers to 40%-50% of wild-type levels. This incomplete recovery may reflect persistent epigenetic inflammatory memory, uncorrected mitochondrial dysfunction, and incomplete restoration of the non-channel functions of CFTR. Moreover, marked interindividual variability in modulator response and persistent nonresponse underscore the need for adjunctive strategies. This review integrates foundational mechanistic studies with recent findings to delineate how CFTR regulates ROS-dependent tissue injury and immune dysregulation and to assess redox-targeted combination therapies designed to complement CFTR modulator monotherapy.

articles.title: Strategic selection of TPD technologies based on disease pathology: from mechanistic diversity to clinical implementation.
articles.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) offersa way to remove disease-associated proteins rather than only inhibit their activity. Its modalities include heterobifunctional degraders, molecular glues, and lysosome-directed strategies, which differ in their mechanisms and accessible substrates. This review examines how disease pathology can guide TPD selection across cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, metabolic syndrome, autoimmune diseases, and infectious diseases. We compare these approaches according to target localization, protein conformation or aggregation state, and the availability of cellular degradation machinery. Representative preclinical studies and clinical programs illustrate both their potential and the limits of current evidence. Clinical translation remains constrained by tissue delivery, pharmacokinetic properties, target and effector selectivity, acquired resistance, and long-term safety. Molecular design and delivery strategies may help address these barriers, but target degradation must be distinguished from demonstrated therapeutic benefit. A pathology-guided framework can therefore support candidate selection and experimental design, while its clinical utility requires validation in specific disease settings.

articles.title: Traditional Paeonia radix alba formulas and their bioactive metabolites: a narrative review focusing on hepatoprotection in chronic liver diseases.
articles.abstract: AIM OF THE REVIEW: Paeoniae radix alba (PRA), a traditional Chinese medicine used for centuries to "soothe the liver" and relieve pain, has attracted increasing attention for its potential role in liver diseases. Emerging pharmacological evidence indicates that PRA exerts hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory effects. This paper reviews traditional Chinese medicine prescriptions containing PRA, its main active metabolites, and their underlying mechanisms in the treatment of liver diseases, and preliminarily summarizes its hepatotoxicity-attenuating mechanisms, to provide directions for further multifaceted research. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We searched Web of Science using the following strategies: AB=(xiaoyaosan OR XYS) AND AB = liver, with analogous searches for the other formulas; AB=(paeoniflorin OR PF OR PAE) AND AB=("Paeonia lactiflora Pall" OR "Paeoniae radix alba" OR PRA) AND AB = liver, with analogous searches for the other metabolites; AB = process* AND AB=("Paeonia lactiflora Pall" OR "Paeoniae radix alba" OR PRA) AND AB = liver; and AB=(hepatotoxicity OR detoxification) AND AB=("Paeonia lactiflora Pall" OR "Paeoniae radix alba" OR PRA). We prioritized studies published within the past 5 years and those with more complete methodological details. RESULTS: PRA and its classic prescriptions, including Xiaoyao San, Shaoyao Gancao Tang, Danggui Shaoyao San and Sini San, have made significant contributions to the treatment of liver diseases. Notably, despite limited current research, PRA can effectively attenuate the hepatotoxicity of other botanical drugs, which is closely associated with its multiple protective effects against liver injury. Therefore, rational and cautious combination therapy should be considered in the clinical application of PRA to maximize its unique advantages and minimize potential risks. CONCLUSION: Within the framework of TCM theory, PRA and its metabolites appear promising for the management of liver diseases and may also mitigate hepatotoxicity associated with certain herbal medicines. Further mechanistic investigations and clinical studies are needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: Tanshinone IIA in colorectal cancer: preclinical mechanisms, therapeutic sensitization, and translational prospects.
articles.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major global health burden, with recurrence, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance limiting durable treatment responses. Tanshinone IIA (Tan IIA), a bioactive diterpene quinone derived from Salvia miltiorrhiza Bunge, has shown broad antitumor activity in preclinical CRC models. This review summarizes its major mechanisms, therapeutic-sensitization effects, and translational potential, while evaluating mechanistic evidence using a three-tier framework encompassing association, functional evidence, and mechanistically supported causality. Tan IIA inhibits proliferation, promotes apoptosis, disrupts mitochondrial and redox homeostasis, suppresses glycolytic adaptation, and modulates autophagy, ferroptosis, invasion, angiogenesis, and the inflammatory tumor microenvironment. It also enhances sensitivity to 5-fluorouracil and oxaliplatin in selected resistant models. Despite these preclinical findings, a substantial exposure gap exists between the nominal concentrations commonly used in CRC cell studies (5-40 μM) and the total plasma peak concentrations reported after oral Danshen administration in healthy volunteers (1.75-25.76 ng/mL). Clinical translation remains challenged by poor aqueous solubility, limited systemic exposure, metabolic clearance, and insufficiently defined exposure-response relationships and safety windows. Future studies should prioritize mechanistic validation and the assessment of pharmacologically active intratumoral exposure, alongside formulation optimization, structural modification, and systematic safety evaluation.

articles.title: Review of oregano essential oils: pharmacological activities and applications.
articles.abstract: Botanical and herbal supplements offer a natural approach to replace antibiotics and are applied for a wide range of purposes. Oregano essential oil (OEO) and its biological active components have attracted attention due to their numerous useful biological activities. As a natural extract, OEO exhibits significant antimicrobial and antioxidant properties, as well as other bioactivities. These potent pharmacological properties enable OEO gradually apply in the fields of food preservation by inhibiting foodborne pathogens and spoilage microbes, thereby extending shelf life while reducing reliance on synthetic additives. Furthermore, OEO is widely used in livestock farming as a natural feed additive that enhance growth performance and rumen health, offering a sustainable alternative to chemical growth promoters. This review summarizes the chemical composition and bioactivity profiles of OEO, with particular emphasis on its application in food preservation and livestock farming as a potential alternative to antibiotics and growth promoters.

articles.title: PD-1 and its ligands in ILC2-mediated airway inflammation in asthma: context-dependent mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
articles.abstract: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) contribute to type 2 asthma through rapid production of interleukin-5 and interleukin-13, but the inhibitory pathways that restrain pathogenic ILC2 activity remain incompletely defined. Most evidence for programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)-mediated inhibition of ILC2s comes from murine models, humanized mice, and stimulated or expanded human cells; cell-resolved expression and functional engagement of PD-1 have not been established in freshly isolated airway ILC2s from well-characterized asthma cohorts. In available experimental systems, PD-1 engagement suppresses ILC2 proliferation and cytokine production, whereas programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) displayed by ILC2s can act outwardly on PD-1-positive CD4-positive T cells. Programmed death-ligand 2 (PD-L2) can inhibit isolated ILC2s through PD-1, but its whole-lung effects also involve dendritic-cell IL-12 regulation and RGMb-dependent respiratory tolerance. Interpretation therefore depends on the ligand-bearing and responding cells, ligand form, tissue compartment, disease stage, and asthma endotype. This review examines cell-intrinsic PD-1 signaling, ligand-specific cellular interactions, immunometabolic regulation, and translational constraints. The current evidence supports preclinical investigation rather than clinical readiness; direct validation in human airway ILC2s, definition of receptor-proximal signaling, and a predictive biomarker are prerequisites for therapeutic development.

articles.title: From recognition to delivery: nucleic acid aptamers in miRNA-related diagnosis and therapy of hepatocellular carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common primary malignant liver tumour, remains a major clinical challenge because of its low early diagnosis rate and high post-treatment recurrence. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play key regulatory roles in HCC development and progression and are potential liquid biopsy biomarkers and therapeutic targets. However, the low abundance and instability of miRNAs in body fluids, together with the limitations of conventional detection methods, have hindered their clinical translation. Nucleic acid aptamers, owing to their high affinity, specificity, and ease of chemical modification, are valuable in miRNA-related detection and targeted delivery. This narrative review summarises technical strategies for aptamer-based and aptamer-inspired detection of HCC-associated miRNAs, as well as aptamer-guided miRNA delivery systems in HCC therapy. Importantly, most aptamers used in HCC research do not directly bind miRNAs; instead, they target HCC cells, surface proteins, or exosomes, whereas miRNAs serve as detection analytes or therapeutic cargo. It analyses the design logic and potential integration pathways of "recognition-delivery" platforms, while distinguishing conceptual integration from experimentally validated single-platform systems. Challenges and future directions are also discussed.

articles.title: Crosstalk between Nrf2 and miRNAs in oxidative stress, cancer progression, and therapy resistance.
articles.abstract: Oxidative stress (OS) is a key feature of a wide range of human disorders, including aging and cancer. The nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2; NFE2L2) is the master regulator of antioxidant responses via antioxidant response element (ARE)-driven gene expression. Its activity is regulated by Keap1. Under basal conditions, Keap1 binds Nrf2, promoting its degradation; OS disrupts this interaction, enabling Nrf2 stabilization, nuclear translocation, and activation of NRF2 regulated. While protecting in normal cells, persistent activation of Nrf2 in cancer promotes chemoresistance and tumor progression. microRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators of Nrf2, via binding to its 3'untranslated region. Databases such as miRBase and Human MiRNA Disease Database, which catalogue thousands of miRNA-disease associations, highlight the complexity and biological relevance of this regulatory network. Several tumor-suppressive miRNAs downregulate Nrf2 and attenuate ARE activity, thereby increasing OS sensitivity, apoptosis, and responsiveness to chemotherapy. Conversely, Nrf2 modulates miRNA networks, forming feedback loops that fine-tune redox homeostasis. While transient Nrf2 activation is generally cytoprotective, sustained Nrf2 hyperactivation in cancer promotes chemoresistance, radioresistance, metabolic reprogramming, metastasis, and poor prognosis, underscoring the need for strategies aimed at limiting Nrf2 signaling and its downstream effects. Given its multifaceted role, Nrf2 has emerged as a promising therapeutic target. Natural Nrf2 modulators and miRNA-based therapeutics (mimics/inhibitors) represent promising strategies to restore redox balance, suppress tumor progression, and overcome multidrug resistance. This review highlights the bidirectional crosstalk between Nrf2 and miRNAs and discusses its therapeutic potential in cancer.

articles.title: Multidimensional analysis of the pathological mechanisms of infantile hemangioma: metabolic reprogramming, immune remodeling, and programmed cell death.
articles.abstract: Infantile hemangioma (IH) is a common benign vascular tumor of infancy. Its self-limiting course, which progresses from proliferation to involution, involves aberrant angiogenesis, altered cell fate, and remodeling of the lesional microenvironment. Hypoxia/HIF-VEGF, PI3K/AKT, MAPK/ERK, and Notch signaling pathways contribute to vascular formation and cellular differentiation. During the proliferative phase, hemangioma endothelial cells (HemECs) undergo metabolic reprogramming characterized by enhanced glycolysis and altered amino acid metabolism, including pathways involving glutamine, arginine, glycine, and serine. Macrophages, mast cells, T cells, and their associated cytokines also shape a proangiogenic immune microenvironment. During the involuting phase, the transition of hemangioma stem cells (HemSCs) toward an adipogenic fate, together with changes in lesional cell composition, contributes to fibrofatty tissue remodeling. At the same time, the immune microenvironment undergoes stage-dependent remodeling, and processes related to programmed cell death, including apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and autophagy, change accordingly. However, the strength of evidence supporting these processes in IH varies. Current studies have identified specific links among metabolism, immunity, and cell death, but they have not established a fixed, sequential causal cascade; PANoptosis remains an unverified mechanistic hypothesis in IH. Although propranolol is the first-line treatment, variable treatment responses, rebound growth after treatment withdrawal, and refractory lesions remain clinical challenges. Focusing on the transition from proliferation to involution, this review integrates current evidence and potential mechanistic connections to inform research on spontaneous involution and the development of interventions tailored to specific disease stages and cell types.

articles.title: Dissolving and hydrogel-based polymeric microneedles for bacterial keratitis: materials, therapeutic payloads, design-performance relationships, and future perspectives.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Bacterial keratitis (BK) is a major cause of corneal visual impairment. Although topical antibiotics remain the mainstay of treatment, tear turnover, blinking, nasolacrimal drainage, and the corneal epithelial barrier limit drug residence and penetration. Polymeric microneedles, particularly dissolving and hydrogel-based systems, may enhance ocular residence of therapeutic agents and enable controlled or sustained drug release. AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes corneal anatomy and ocular drug-delivery barriers, outlines the pathophysiology of bacterial keratitis, and evaluates microneedle platforms developed for ocular applications, with emphasis on dissolving and hydrogel-based polymeric systems for bacterial keratitis. A focused search of PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect was undertaken, supplemented by a search of Google Scholar to identify additional relevant studies. Relevant studies were compared according to polymer composition, microneedle dimensions and density, penetration depth, dissolution or swelling, and release kinetics. Polymer design-property relationships, including the effects of concentration, molecular weight, crosslinking, biodegradability, and post-administration polymer fate, are also discussed. EXPERT OPINION: Polymeric microneedles offer a promising strategy for overcoming corneal delivery barriers, but clinical translation will depend on reproducible manufacturing, mechanical and ocular safety, sterilization and storage stability, user-friendly application, and robust clinical evidence demonstrating advantages over optimized topical therapies.

articles.title: A bibliometric analysis of bibliometric research in pharmacology.
articles.abstract: Bibliometric papers are among the fastest-growing article types in pharmacology, yet the genre itself has seldom been examined with its own tools. We retrieved all Scopus records in the Pharmacology, Toxicology and Pharmaceutics subject area that mentioned 'bibliometric' or 'scientometric' in the title, abstract or keywords (n = 1979; search date 27 October 2026). After a five-step screening procedure that removed errata, duplicate versions and records outside the biomedical and pharmaceutical domain, 1823 documents were analysed. Output grew by 24.5% per year between 2006 and 2025 (doubling time 3.2 years). China-affiliated authors contributed 54.1% of documents but co-authored internationally on only 10.3% of them. Titles framed around 'hotspots', 'frontiers' or 'trends' rose from 9.1% of documents published up to 2020 to 34.4% of those published in 2023-2025, and a formulaic hotspot-plus-mapping title accounted for 29.8% of recent output. Production was concentrated in seven core journals, led by Frontiers in Pharmacology. In a negative binomial model of 913 articles and reviews (2015-2024), review status (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 2.01), international co-authorship (1.64) and acknowledged funding (1.38) were associated with higher citation counts and Chinese language publication with lower counts (0.16). The crude open access advantage (IRR 1.37) disappeared after adjustment for language, and template titles showed no independent association. The model explained only a small share of citation variance, and the associations are observational. The recent expansion of the genre reflects volume more than distinctive impact, which supports asking bibliometric submissions for a pharmacological question, transparent reporting and interpretation beyond descriptive mapping.

articles.title: An overlooked Gα subunit in cancer: GNA14-driven signaling rewires tumor growth and angiogenesis.
articles.abstract: GNA14, a key member of the Gαq/11 subfamily, functions as a G-protein α-subunit involved in diverse cellular signaling processes. Its expression is primarily regulated by genetic mutations and promoter methylation. Recent studies have demonstrated that GNA14 is aberrantly expressed in a wide range of tumor types, including vascular tumors, hepatocellular carcinoma, and endometrial carcinoma. By modulating key signaling pathways such as MAPK/JNK, Notch1/RB, and NF-κB, GNA14 plays a crucial role in regulating tumor cell proliferation, apoptosis, invasion, metastasis, and angiogenesis. By integrating and analyzing current research, this article provides a systematic overview of the molecular structure and functions of GNA14, as well as its expression patterns and mechanistic roles in vascular tumors and various cancers. It further explores the potential of GNA14 as a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target, offering new theoretical foundations and research perspectives for early tumor detection, precision therapy, and prognostic assessment.

articles.title: Machine learning prediction of cyclosporine nephrotoxicity in pediatric patients using therapeutic drug monitoring and clinical data.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cyclosporine A (CsA) nephrotoxicity is a dose-limiting toxicity in pediatric immunosuppression, and early identification of children at risk of CsA-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) remains an unmet clinical need. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: In retrospective cohorts of CsA-treated inpatients undergoing therapeutic drug monitoring (352 children; 342 adults), a regularized logistic-regression model was compared with six machine-learning classifiers under five feature-selection schemes, three small-sample strategies were evaluated, and adult-child transferability was assessed on 95 aligned features. A 14-variable model was externally validated in an independent pediatric cohort (n = 257). RESULTS: Regularized logistic regression achieved the best discrimination in children (hold-out AUC 0.800) and adults (hold-out AUC 0.956), with complex models overfitting. Adult and pediatric risk architectures differed fundamentally, with transfer AUCs near chance (≈0.6). The 14-variable model retained discrimination on external validation (AUC 0.784, 95% CI 0.656-0.912). CONCLUSIONS: On small clinical datasets, regularization rather than complexity determines predictive performance. We provide an interpretable, TDM-integrated pediatric CsA-AKI model, deployed as an online calculator, supporting early risk stratification in pediatric CsA therapy.

articles.title: Repurposing of LSD - a scoping review of current clinical trials.
articles.abstract: LSD was banned in many countries for a very long time and was purchased by users for recreational use on the black market. Since 2014, there has been steady growth in interest in its potential use in treating pain disorders and neuropsychiatric conditions. Consequently, an increasing number of studies on the repurposing of LSD have been conducted; in some cases, the conditions treated corresponded to those in studies from the 1950s and 1960s, while in others, the scope was expanded to include new areas of application. Clinicaltrials.org, ANZCTR, the Netherlands trial registry and PubMed research were used to identify the clinical trials. For this publication, 51 studies were analyzed, 25 of which were published. The goal is to map the status quo of the current state of research and analyze the study design. The analysis parameters included study design, conditions, sponsoring, study location, and overall outcome. Most studies are still in phase 1, followed by phase 2. Three phase 3 studies are currently being conducted. The condition entities were: alcohol use disorder (n = 1), anxiety disorders (n = 3), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) (n = 1), cluster headache (chronic and non-chronic, n = 2); major depressive disorder (n = 4), premenstrual disorders (premenstrual syndrome (PMS)) and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) (n = 1), palliative care/end-of-life distress (n = 2). The most used dosage is 100 µg. Most studies are interventional RCTs using inactive placebos and are conducted in Switzerland, followed by the USA, the Netherlands, and New Zealand/Australia. The outcome of the published trials was analyzed further. So far, LSD shows possible benefits in the treatment of anxiety disorders and major depressive disorders. The effectiveness of microdosing could not be adequately proven, and the results varied greatly, which could be due to differences in dosage and administration. More detailed studies, particularly phase 2 or phase 3 studies, are needed to make more informed statements.

articles.title: Dexmedetomidine-associated bradycardia in perioperative and critical care settings: a cross-database pharmacovigilance study using FAERS and JADER.
articles.abstract: Dexmedetomidine (DEX) is a highly selective α2-adrenoceptor agonist widely used for sedation in perioperative and critical care settings. Although bradycardia is a recognised adverse effect, its temporal reporting patterns and associated clinical characteristics remain incompletely characterised. This study investigated DEX-associated bradycardia using two independent spontaneous reporting systems. We conducted a retrospective pharmacovigilance study using the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and the Japanese Adverse Drug Event Report (JADER) database from 2004Q1 to 2025Q3. Reports suggestive of perioperative or critical care use were identified using predefined proxy indicators. Disproportionality analyses were performed to detect cardiovascular safety signals. Time to onset (TTO) patterns were evaluated using Weibull modelling, and factors associated with bradycardia reporting were examined using multivariable case-non-case logistic regression. Sensitivity analyses assessed the consistency of the findings. Among 2505 DEX reports, 717 involved bradycardia-associated events (FAERS, n = 327; JADER, n = 390). Bradycardia showed prominent disproportionality signals in both databases. Among 198 reports with valid TTO data, the median onset time was 0 days in both databases, with similar Weibull shape parameters (FAERS, β = 0.849; JADER, β = 0.847), suggesting early clustering of reported events. Pre-existing cardiovascular disease showed the strongest adjusted association with bradycardia reporting (OR 4.88, 95% CI 3.92-6.09), followed by concomitant opioid use (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.37-2.22) and β-adrenoceptor blocker exposure (OR 1.85, 95% CI 1.08-3.13). These associations were generally consistent across sensitivity analyses. DEX-associated bradycardia showed consistent reporting signals across FAERS and JADER, with reported onset times frequently concentrated near treatment initiation. Cardiovascular disease and concomitant opioid or β-adrenoceptor blocker exposure were associated with higher odds of bradycardia reporting. Although spontaneous reporting data cannot establish causality or quantify incidence, these findings provide complementary post-marketing evidence supporting careful cardiovascular assessment and haemodynamic monitoring during DEX administration.

articles.title: Exploring candidate molecular links between acetamiprid-related targets and osteosarcoma-associated signatures using network toxicology, transcriptomic analyses, and in vitro validation.
articles.abstract: Acetamiprid (ACE) has been implicated not only in bone metabolic disorders but also in the development of various cancers. Nevertheless, its role in osteosarcoma (OS) and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. We integrated network toxicology, transcriptomics, molecular docking, single-cell analysis, machine learning, and preliminary in vitro experiments to explore potential links between ACE-related targets and OS-associated signatures. We identified 219 ACE-related targets and 3299 OS-associated genes, including 62 overlapping candidates. Functional enrichment analyses highlighted inflammatory pathways, including TNF and IL-17 signaling. Exploratory machine learning analyses prioritized CAT and MPO, with CAT showing comparatively more consistent support across subsequent analyses and MPO showing less consistent cross-dataset performance. CAT demonstrated dataset-level discriminatory performance in the evaluated public transcriptomic datasets. Immune-context and single-cell analyses further characterized associations between candidate-gene expression, inferred immune-cell composition, and cellular distribution. Molecular docking generated computationally plausible ACE-protein binding poses but did not establish direct target engagement. In vitro, ACE treatment altered cellular metabolic activity, wound closure, and CAT expression in U-2 OS cells under the tested conditions. CAT emerged as a prioritized candidate molecular feature associated with ACE-related cellular responses and OS-associated molecular signatures. These findings are exploratory and do not establish a causal relationship between ACE exposure and OS development or progression.
