This presents a significant clinical challenge, leading to unnecessary polypharmacy and increased risk of adverse events. Overuse in the hospital settings is well documented. However, there is limited evidence on prescribing patterns for outpatients in Saudi Arabia. This study investigated PPI prescription frequency among outpatients and assessed demographics, specialty-group, and diagnosis associations with prescription rates after accounting for observable time. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective cohort analysis was conducted using electronic health records from the calendar year of 2023. Adult outpatients who received at least one PPI prescription were included. The outcome was the number of PPI prescriptions per patient. Descriptive statistics, univariate analyses, and Poisson regression with robust standard errors were used to identify the primary demographic and clinical predictors of prescription frequency. RESULTS: A cohort of 5586 patients was analysed, accounting for 30,748 discrete prescription events. Females constituted 55.2% of the cohort, and the mean age was 52.4 years. Pantoprazole accounted for 73.5% of all cases, dominating the volume of prescription. Although 46.8% of patients required only one prescription, the median number of PPI prescriptions was two per patient and 299 patients (5.4%) received five or more prescriptions. In adjusted analyses of patients with complete covariate data (n = 5,482), prescription rates increased with age (Model A IRR 1.005 per year, 95% CI, 1.004-1.006; p < 0.001) and were higher among Non-Saudi Arab patients than Saudi patients (IRR, 1.085; 95% CI, 1.035-1.137; p < 0.001). In the diagnosis model, systemic lupus erythematosus (IRR, 1.249), type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications (IRR, 1.137), and essential hypertension (IRR, 1.176) were associated with higher prescription rates. CONCLUSION: Outpatients being managed for complex cardiovascular and metabolic conditions demonstrated elevated and sustained PPI prescriptions. These findings support the need for improved medication review and rational prescribing strategies. Pharmacist-led stewardship and indication-based review within electronic health records may be appropriate areas for future intervention. Future studies should assess indication, dose, treatment duration and guidelines compliance.

articles.title: Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of RXRA-overexpressing chronic myeloid leukemia cells identifies protein kinase D as a candidate target for imatinib sensitization.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Retinoid-X-receptor alpha (RXRA) is downregulated in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). We previously demonstrated that overexpression of RXRA sensitizes CML cells to imatinib, but the mechanisms underlying this effect remain undefined. OBJECTIVE: To characterize the molecular programs associated with RXRA-mediated imatinib sensitization through integrated transcriptomic-proteomic profiling, and to identify and examine pharmacologically actionable downstream effectors in CML cell lines and primary patient-derived CD34+ cells. METHODS: RXRA-overexpressing (RXRA-OE) and empty vector (EV) LAMA84 cells were profiled by RNA sequencing and mass spectrometry-based proteomics. Four concordantly downregulated candidates (PRKD1, UCHL1, FSCN1 and NTRK3), prioritized by magnitude of concordant downregulation, biological relevance and inhibitor availability, were confirmed by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting. Pharmacological inhibition of each candidate combined with imatinib was assessed in CML cell lines, primary CML CD34+ cells and healthy-donor CD34+ controls. RESULTS: RXRA overexpression produced 7,053 differentially expressed transcripts and 1,668 differentially abundant proteins (technical triplicates of one sample per group), with 711 concordant gene-protein pairs (Pearson r = 0.64). RXRA-overexpressing cells scored higher for genes downregulated in hematopoietic stem cells and for the granulocyte-monocyte progenitor signature, with enriched myeloid gene sets and reduced expression of receptor tyrosine kinase and growth-factor signaling genes. Enzymes of glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and sterol biosynthesis were downregulated, while lipid catabolic genes were upregulated. Among the four candidates, the serine/threonine kinase PRKD1 and the deubiquitinase UCHL1 emerged as candidate imatinib-sensitizing targets: the pan-PKD inhibitor CRT0066101 and the UCHL1 inhibitor LDN-57444 each synergized with imatinib and reduced clonogenic potential. PRKD1 protein was detected in all four CML cell lines tested. Combined PKD inhibition and imatinib reduced the viability and colony-forming capacity of primary CML CD34+ cells. In healthy-donor CD34+ cells the live-cell fraction did not differ between treatments (n = 5), and colony formation was assessed in two donors; these comparisons were limited by sample size and selectivity for CML cells was not established. CONCLUSION: Integrated multi-omics associates RXRA overexpression with myeloid lineage-associated and metabolic expression signatures in imatinib-sensitized CML cells, and identifies PRKD1 as a candidate effector whose pharmacological targeting with a pan-PKD inhibitor enhances imatinib efficacy in vitro.

articles.title: Oral anticoagulants and the risk of acute kidney injury: a retrospective real-world cohort study using overlap propensity score weighting.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy, initially described in association with warfarin, has increasingly been reported with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). However, the comparative risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) within 30 days of treatment initiation between warfarin and DOACs across a broad spectrum of clinical indications remains unclear. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included patients newly initiated on DOACs or warfarin between January 2014 and May 2025 at the Third Xiangya Hospital of Central South University. Overlap propensity score weighting, with weights derived from a generalized boosted model incorporating 81 baseline covariates, balanced the treatment groups. Weighted logistic regression compared the risk of AKI within 30 days of OAC initiation, defined by KDIGO criteria. Sensitivity analyses included inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and logistic regression-derived overlap weighting, each with or without doubly robust covariate adjustment. RESULTS: Among 6 876 patients (5 048 DOAC users; 1 828 warfarin users), DOAC initiation was associated with a higher risk of AKI than warfarin after overlap weighting (OR: 1.346, 95% CI: 1.057-1.715; p = 0.016), and with severe AKI (stage 2-3; OR: 1.694, 95% CI: 1.013-2.832; p = 0.044), whereas stage 1 AKI did not differ significantly. The association persisted after additional covariate adjustment (OR: 1.363, 95% CI: 1.068-1.740; p = 0.013) and across alternative propensity score models, although the unadjusted IPTW model did not. By indication, the association was significant for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF) (OR: 1.566, 95% CI: 1.034-2.369; p = 0.034) but not for venous thromboembolism (VTE) treatment or prophylaxis. Among individual DOACs, rivaroxaban was associated with an elevated risk (OR: 1.392, 95% CI: 1.075-1.804; p = 0.012), whereas edoxaban, dabigatran, and apixaban were not. Lower-dose rivaroxaban initiation was associated with an increased risk (OR: 2.792, 95% CI: 1.524-5.114; p = 0.001), whereas higher-dose and off-label use were not. In prespecified subgroup analyses, ORs were above 1 in most strata, but most comparisons were not significant, and no significant interactions were detected. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, may be associated with a higher short-term risk of AKI than warfarin. Given the expanding use of DOACs, medication-specific renal effects warrant further investigation, and close monitoring of renal function may be advisable in high-risk patients after anticoagulation initiation.

articles.title: Engineering a multifunctional LL37-TP5 hybrid peptide with potent antimicrobial endotoxin-neutralizing and anti-inflammatory properties.
articles.abstract: The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance and endotoxin-mediated inflammation highlights the need for alternative therapeutic strategies that combine antibacterial and immunomodulatory functions. Although cathelicidin LL-37 exhibits potent antimicrobial and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-neutralizing activity, its clinical application is limited by cytotoxicity and high production costs. A hybrid peptide, LL37-TP5, was designed by fusing the active LPS-binding region of LL-37 (residues 13-36) with the immunomodulatory penta peptide thymopentin (TP5) to enhance endotoxin-neutralizing activity while reducing host cytotoxicity. Bioinformatics analyses predicted that LL37-TP5 adopt amphipathic α-helical structure with optimized hydrophobicity and a strong net positive (+9) charge. The hybrid peptide was successfully expressed recombinantly in Pichia pastoris (P. pastoris) and purified by Reverse-Phase High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (RP-HPLC), yielding approximately 20.5 mg/L with 95.2% purity, consistent with in silico predictions. Considering the increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance in poultry production, the antibacterial activity of LL37-TP5 was evaluated against major poultry-associated bacterial pathogens. LL37-TP5 exhibited broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, with low minimum inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations. Furthermore, the hybrid peptide showed enhanced LPS-neutralizing activity and significantly suppressed nitric oxide and pro-inflammatory cytokine (IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β) production in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages. Importantly, LL37-TP5 demonstrated markedly reduced cytotoxicity and negligible hemolytic activity compared with parental LL-37. Collectively, our findings indicate that hybridization of LL-37 with TP5 generated a peptide with favorable antimicrobial, endotoxin-neutralizing, and anti-inflammatory properties together with an improved safety profile compared with native LL-37.

articles.title: Sulodexide versus low-molecular-weight heparin in critically ill neonates: a propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Critically ill neonates are at high risk of thrombosis, inflammation, and antimicrobial exposure in the neonatal intensive care unit, but evidence guiding adjunctive anticoagulant selection remains limited. We compared the clinical, laboratory, and safety outcomes associated with sulodexide (SDX) and low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included critically ill neonates treated with sulodexide or low-molecular-weight heparin. Propensity score matching (PSM) yielded 85 matched pairs. The primary outcome was relative percentage change in D-dimer from baseline to treatment end. Secondary outcomes included other coagulation, hematological, blood-gas, and respiratory-support measures. Inflammatory status and antimicrobial defined daily doses (DDDs) were exploratory outcomes. Bleeding events first documented after treatment initiation were assessed as safety outcomes. RESULTS: Among 234 eligible neonates, 85 matched pairs were analyzed. D-dimer change did not differ significantly between groups [-70.2% (-82.0, -50.5) vs. -72.0% (-87.1, -42.2); between-group effect, 1.4 percentage points; 95% CI, -8.3 to 9.7; P = 0.765], and no other coagulation, hematological, or blood-gas outcomes differed significantly. Among neonates with abnormal baseline inflammatory status, CRP/hs-CRP improvement occurred in 12/12 (100.0%) and 7/11 (63.6%) in the SDX and LMWH groups, respectively (P = 0.037), suggesting a potential difference in inflammatory response. SDX remained associated with lower observed DDDs after multivariable adjustment, although this association was not robust in calendar-period sensitivity analyses. Bleeding was first documented after treatment initiation in 24/85 (28.2%) SDX-treated and 18/85 (21.2%) LMWH-treated neonates, respectively. Among neonates with bleeding, first documentation occurred during active treatment in 9/24 (37.5%) and 14/18 (77.8%), respectively. CONCLUSION: No significant between-group differences were observed in the primary D-dimer or other coagulation outcomes. A higher proportion of CRP/hs-CRP improvement was observed in the SDX group, although this finding was exploratory and based on a small subgroup. The lower observed DDDs were not robust to calendar-period analyses and should not be attributed to a drug-specific effect. Bleeding was numerically more frequent in the SDX group overall, whereas a greater proportion of bleeding cases in the LMWH group were first documented during active treatment. The observed timing pattern does not establish a causal relationship with treatment. These retrospective findings require cautious interpretation and prospective confirmation.

articles.title: A tumor-responsive nanoplatform orchestrating multiplexed macrophage engagers and immune checkpoint blockade for triple-negative breast cancer immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains a formidable clinical challenge due to its profound inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity and highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), which severely limit the efficacy of standard immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapies. To overcome these multifactorial barriers, we engineered a dual-responsive, targeted lipid nanoparticle platform, denoted as R-DCPA-GPL-LNP@mET, designed to holistically orchestrate innate and adaptive anti-tumor immunity. METHODS: This multifunctional nanoplatform co-delivers multiplexed mRNAs encoding bispecific macrophage engagers that simultaneously target Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) and Trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2 (TROP2), ensuring comprehensive engagement of heterogeneous TNBC cells. The nanocarrier utilizes a pH-responsive charge-reversal lipid (DCPA) to accelerate robust endosomal escape in the acidic TME, alongside a glutathione (GSH)-cleavable anti-PD-L1 antibody tethered to the surface for tumor-selective ICB release. RESULTS: Upon systemic administration, the translated bispecific engagers physically bridge tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) with TNBC cells, reprograming TAMs toward a tumoricidal M1 phenotype, triggering highly efficient phagocytosis, and neutralizing oncogenic PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathways. Concurrently, the localized release of anti-PD-L1 synergizes with this innate immune activation to profoundly remodel the TME, driving the extensive infiltration of cytotoxic T lymphocytes and Natural Killer cells while depleting immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells. In an orthotopic 4T1 TNBC murine model, this multiplexed, spatiotemporal intervention induced marked tumor regression with a favorable preliminary safety profile over the 22-day observation period. DISCUSSION: Collectively, these preclinical findings support further development of this multiplexed, dual-responsive nanoplatform as a promising strategy for heterogeneous and immunosuppressive solid tumors.

articles.title: Paeoniflorin ameliorates Parkinson's disease by promoting autophagy to inhibit A1 phenotype astrocyte activation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Autophagy dysfunction and astrocyte activation are considered important factors contributing to dopaminergic neuron death and the progression of Parkinson's disease. Paeoniflorin, a monoterpene glycoside, exhibits multiple pharmacological effects, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory properties. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of paeoniflorin on Parkinson's disease and the underlying molecular mechanisms. METHODS: Using the 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced PD mouse model, the pharmacological effects of paeoniflorin were evaluated by behavioral assessment, immunohistochemical staining, and Western blotting. For the in vitro experiments, A1-phenotype astrocytes were induced with supernatant from LPS-stimulated microglia, and the regulatory effects of paeoniflorin on astrocyte activation were evaluated by immunofluorescence and Western blotting. RESULTS: Paeoniflorin ameliorated dopaminergic neuron damage and motor dysfunction in the MPTP-induced PD mouse model. Furthermore, paeoniflorin inhibited the activation of A1-phenotype astrocytes by promoting autophagy. CONCLUSION: Paeoniflorin ameliorates Parkinson's disease pathology by promoting autophagy and inhibiting the activation of A1-phenotype astrocytes. These findings uncover potential therapeutic targets and intervention strategies for Parkinson's disease. Keywords: Parkinson's disease; paeoniflorin; autophagy; A1-phenotype astrocytes; mTOR.

articles.title: Magnesium cantharidate suppresses hepatocellular carcinoma progression and modulates tumor-associated macrophage polarization: potential involvement of ERK1/2 signaling and de novo serine synthesis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in which M2-like tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) contribute to tumor progression. De novo serine synthesis is increasingly recognized as an important regulator of macrophage polarization. Magnesium cantharidate (MC) exhibits anti-HCC activity; however, whether MC regulates TAM polarization through the de novo serine synthesis pathway remains unclear. METHODS: HCC-derived TAMs were generated using conditioned media from HCC cells and treated with MC. Macrophage polarization, metabolomic and transcriptomic alterations, de novo serine synthesis and activation of the ERK signaling pathway were evaluated. Pharmacological inhibition and siRNA-mediated knockdown of PHGDH were used for functional validation. TAM-conditioned media were used to assess their effects on HCC cells, and key findings were further validated in a Hep3B/TAMs xenograft model. RESULTS: MC significantly inhibited the growth of Hep3B/TAM xenografts. Additionally, MC significantly reduced CD206+ TAMs and decreased the expression of the M2-associated markers Arg-1, IL-10 and TGFB1 in vivo and in vitro. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses showed that MC altered serine-associated metabolic programs in TAMs. Moreover, MC reduced the expression of key enzymes involved in de novo serine synthesis (PHGDH, PSAT1 and PSPH) in vivo and in vitro. Pharmacological inhibition or knockdown of PHGDH further enhanced the suppressive effect of MC on M2-like TAM polarization. Moreover, conditioned media from MC-treated TAMs inhibited HCC cell proliferation, migration and invasion, and these effects were further strengthened by PHGDH inhibition or knockdown. Molecular docking suggested favorable binding potential between MC and ERK1/2. MC reduced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in xenograft tumors and in TAMs. Additionally, pharmacological ERK1/2 inhibition further decreased PHGDH, PSAT1 and PSPH expression and potentiated the inhibitory effect of MC on the expression of key enzymes involved in de novo serine synthesis. CONCLUSION: MC could suppress HCC xenograft growth and modulate M2-like TAM-associated phenotypes, accompanied by alterations in serine metabolism and ERK1/2 signaling. These findings suggested the potential involvement of ERK1/2 signaling and de novo serine synthesis-related pathways in the antitumor effects of MC.

articles.title: Justicia procumbens suppresses high-fat diet-induced weight gain in mice and adipogenesis in 3T3-L1 cells with inhibition of AKT and STAT3 phosphorylation.
articles.abstract: Obesity is a major public health concern, and the long-term use of current pharmacological therapies can be constrained by adverse effects. Therefore, natural products with potential applicability to obesity management are of growing interest. Here, we investigated the anti-obesity effects of an extract of Justicia procumbens (JE), a traditionally used medicinal plant, and its underlying mechanisms. Oral administration of JE in a high-fat diet-induced obese mouse model significantly reduced body weight gain, white adipose tissue mass, hepatic lipid accumulation, and circulating triglyceride levels. Chemical profiling of JE followed by chromatographic purification and structural characterization identified seven lignans and lignan glycosides, including two previously undescribed lignan glycosides. Network pharmacology analysis highlighted phosphorylation-related signaling pathways associated with adipogenesis, particularly PI3K-AKT and JAK-STAT signaling, as candidate mechanisms of JE action. Consistent with these predictions, JE suppressed adipogenic differentiation and attenuated AKT-p70S6K and STAT3 phosphorylation in 3T3-L1 preadipocytes and white adipose tissue. Functional screening further identified four lignan compounds with anti-adipogenic activity that differentially attenuated AKT or STAT3 phosphorylation. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that JE suppresses adipogenesis and attenuates obesity-associated metabolic abnormalities, highlighting its potential as a plant-derived candidate for obesity management.

articles.title: Human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes alleviate cerebral Palsy-Associated neuronal damage via TSC1/mTOR/ULK1 autophagy suppression and PINK1/Parkin mitophagy restoration.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cerebral palsy (CP) from perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury lacks effective therapies. Human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (hAMSC-exos) show neuroprotective potential, but their mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the effects and molecular pathways of hAMSC-exos in a neonatal rat CP model and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) neuronal model. METHODS: hAMSC-exos were isolated and characterised. Severe CP was induced in postnatal day 21 rats by carotid ligation and hypoxia; hAMSC-exos or vehicle were given via tail vein 24 h later. Brain histology, ultrastructure, TSC1/mTOR/ULK1 pathway proteins, and apoptosis were assessed. In vitro, cortical neurons underwent OGD/R with or without exosomes; mitochondrial function (ATP, ROS, membrane potential), morphology, dynamics proteins (DRP1, FIS1, MFN1, MFN2), and PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy were evaluated. RESULTS: hAMSC-exos significantly ameliorated cortical neuronal degeneration, Nissl loss, and mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, and reduced autophagosome accumulation. They reversed CP-induced TSC1 upregulation, restored mTOR phosphorylation, and decreased ULK1 phosphorylation, correlating with fewer apoptotic neurons. In vitro, exosomes restored ATP content, reduced mitochondrial ROS, and normalised membrane potential. OGD/R caused excessive mitochondrial elongation via MFN1 upregulation; exosomes selectively downregulated MFN1 without affecting fission proteins (DRP1, FIS1). Moreover, exosomes restored impaired PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, increasing co-localisation of phospho-PINK1, phospho-Parkin, and LAMP1 with mitochondria, and rescued their phosphorylated protein levels. CONCLUSION: hAMSC-exos protect against hypoxic-ischaemic injury through coordinated regulation of mitochondrial quality control, involving suppression of excessive TSC1/mTOR/ULK1-mediated autophagy (in vivo) and restoration of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy (in vitro), collectively preserving mitochondrial integrity and reducing neuronal apoptosis. These findings support hAMSC-exos as a promising cell-free therapeutic strategy for CP.

articles.title: Protective effects of ivermectin against ischemia-reperfusion-induced ovarian injury in rats.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ovarian ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury induces severe tissue damage through oxidative stress and inflammation, and DNA damage. This study investigated the protective effects of short- and long-term ivermectin application against ovarian I/R injury in rats. METHODS: Twenty-four female Wistar albino rats were divided into four groups: sham operation (SOG), ovarian I/R (OIR), long-term ivermectin-applied I/R (LIOIR), and short-term ivermectin-applied I/R (SIOIR). Ovarian torsion was maintained for 3 h before detorsion. Ivermectin (2 mg/kg, orally) was administered for 3 or 6 days. Ovarian malondialdehyde (MDA), total glutathione (tGSH), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and catalase (CAT) were measured. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), and 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) were also performed. RESULTS: OIR increased MDA and reduced tGSH, SOD, and CAT. Three-day ivermectin pretreatment normalized oxidative stress marker levels to values comparable to those in the sham group, whereas six-day pretreatment provided no significant protection. Follicular degeneration was pronounced in OIR and LIOIR but markedly attenuated in SIOIR. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated preserved COX-1 expression and reduced COX-2 and 8-OHdG immunoreactivity following short-term ivermectin pretreatment. CONCLUSION: Short-term ivermectin effectively protected ovarian tissue against experimental I/R injury by reducing oxidative stress, inflammation, and DNA damage, whereas prolonged pretreatment failed to provide comparable protection, supporting its therapeutic potential.

articles.title: Quality, readability, and information fidelity of large language model-generated versus physician-authored informed-consent content for targeted therapies: a blinded, paired comparative study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the content quality of basic information, risks, benefits, and alternative options in informed consent forms for targeted therapy generated by large language models (LLMs) versus those drafted by physicians, and to evaluate informational fidelity and reading level. METHODS: This study used a single-center, retrospective, paired-case, blinded multi-evaluator design. We enrolled 70 adult patients who received targeted therapy in the Department of Rheumatology at Beijing Tongren Hospital during 2025. LLM texts were generated using DeepSeek-V4-pro based on identical de-identified case data and standardized prompts, and corresponding physician texts were extracted from electronic records. Three rheumatologists performed blinded scoring using a scale comprising 8 domains and 13 items. Reading level and informational errors were assessed using CRIE 3.0 and source tracing. RESULTS: A total of 140 texts were analyzed. The LLM arm achieved a higher median overall quality score than the physician arm (60 vs. 50; adjusted mean difference 9.95, 95% CI 9.36 to 10.54; p < 0.01), with higher scores for risks, benefits, and alternatives (all adjusted p < 0.01). The LLM arm also exhibited higher reading level scores (7.87 vs. 7.10; p < 0.01) and a higher rate of hallucinations (27.1% vs. 0; p < 0.01). No statistically significant between-arm differences were found for inaccuracies or omissions. CONCLUSION: In this exploratory study, according to a locally developed assessment framework, LLM-generated texts received higher composite evaluator ratings and more consistently covered predefined informed consent content domains. However, they more frequently contained unsupported patient-specific inferences and imposed a greater reading burden. LLMs may be useful for generating structured drafts and checking coverage of predefined content, but they should not be used to produce final informed consent documents without physician review and item-by-item verification. These findings require further validation using patient-centered outcomes.

articles.title: Distinguishing smoke exposure from emerging pathology: temporal metabolomic profiling in a rat model of cigarette smoke-induced lung injury.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: COPD is a prevalent, progressive respiratory disorder for which cigarette smoking represents the predominant modifiable risk factor. To distinguish metabolites merely indicative of tobacco exposure from those specifically associated with incipient COPD-related pathological changes, we employed untargeted ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry to comprehensively profile serum and urine metabolomes in a time-stratified rat model of chronic cigarette smoke exposure. This approach enabled systematic characterization of dynamic, time-dependent metabolic perturbations and facilitated the identification of candidate metabolites linked both to smoke exposure and to early-stage lung injury. METHODS: We set up four groups of rat models treated with smoking method at different times to evaluate and understand the development process of COPD from the onset to the stable stage. The animal models were verified by pathological experiments, and the serum and urine of rats were analyzed by mass spectrometry to compare the changes of urine and serum metabolites in different periods of smoking. As a first step toward identifying exposure markers and candidate pathology-related metabolites in at-risk smokers, we sought to identify metabolites associated with cigarette smoke exposure and early smoke-induced pulmonary changes. RESULTS: Four candidate metabolites were identified by non-targeted metabolomic analysis, and receiver work characteristics analysis showed that all types of metabolomic data had high predictive power, with area under the curve values exceeding 0.75. These results suggest that the identified metabolites can distinguish cigarette smoke exposure from unexposed conditions and may be associated with COPD-like pulmonary pathology. CONCLUSION: This study profiled serum and urine metabolites in a time-stratified rat model of cigarette smoke-induced lung injury. Using multivariate and univariate analyses with correction for multiple testing, we identified four metabolites associated with smoke exposure and with emerging smoke-induced lung pathology.

articles.title: Development of a Clinical Decision Support Tool for Drug Dose Adjustment Based on Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate.
Strengthening medicine availability through enhanced international collaboration: Outcomes from a pilot on global regulatory assessment of manufacturing changes.
articles.abstract: Medicine shortages continue to represent a critical global health challenge. While causes are multifactorial, issues can be mitigated by measures that increase manufacturing capacity. However, these require regulatory approval, often across multiple jurisdictions, and between-regulator differences in regulatory systems, data requirements and approval timelines can make global approval complex and time consuming. To address this challenge, the International Coalition of Medicines Regulatory Authorities (ICMRA) launched a pilot programme in which five submissions went through collaborative review of the same chemistry, manufacturing and control (CMC) data by up to eight global regulatory authorities, aiming to deliver harmonized outcomes using science and risk-based assessment principles. A standardized 120-day review process was established, enabling near-simultaneous approvals across participating regions. Most (88%) assessment questions were harmonized; alignment reduced the number of questions by 25% compared with independent reviews. These results demonstrate that global regulatory collaboration can significantly accelerate implementation of manufacturing changes, strengthen supply chains and help to mitigate medicine shortages. Efforts are underway to develop this into a sustainable global regulatory approach.

articles.title: Association Between Urinary pH and Vancomycin-Associated Acute Kidney Injury.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Vancomycin (VCM) is an antibiotic widely used to treat Gram-positive bacterial infections but commonly causes severe acute kidney injury (AKI). Because VCM contains an amino group with a pKa of 7.2 and has an isoelectric point of 7.2, its ionization state may depend on urinary pH, potentially influencing susceptibility to VCM-associated AKI (VCM-AKI). OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to clarify the relationship between urinary pH and VCM-AKI. METHODS: This study analysed patients whose urinary pH was measured during intravenous VCM treatment at Chiba University Hospital between April 2013 and December 2024. The onset of VCM-AKI was determined using a modified KDIGO 2012 criteria. A multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with VCM-AKI. RESULTS: The number of analysed patients without and with AKI were 437 and 50, respectively. The multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that intensive care unit admission, loop diuretics use, serum VCM trough concentration and urinary pH (odds ratio, 0.69; 95% confidence interval, 0.48-0.98; p = 0.04) were significantly associated with VCM-AKI. CONCLUSIONS: The findings of this retrospective study suggest that urinary pH is significantly associated with VCM-AKI in hospitalized patients. Further prospective studies are needed to validate this association.

articles.title: Nicotine dose effect function and actions of monoamine oxidase inhibiting drug on nicotine self-administration in female rats.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Rationale Tobacco is addictive and nicotine is the primary psychoactive chemical in tobacco. Nicotine is reliably self-administered in rat models, but, unlike stimulants and opiates, it is only weakly reinforcing. OBJECTIVES: Are there other tobacco chemicals that potentiate nicotine self-administration? METHODS: Adult female Sprague-Dawley rats were examined for impacts of monoamine oxidase inhibiting (MAOi) chemicals found in tobacco on nicotine self-administration (SA). In addition, a range of nicotine doses were investigated to determine potential impact of lowering nicotine levels modestly or substantially on its SA. The MAOi compounds, harmane, harmaline and 1-ethyl-β-carboline (EBC), were given to rats offered any of three different nicotine doses (3, 10 or 30 µg/kg/infusion). RESULTS: There was an inverted U-shaped dose-effect function of nicotine self-administration. Reduction of nicotine dose from the benchmark 30 to 10 µg/kg/infusion significantly increased self-administered infusions. A further lowering of nicotine from 10 to 3 µg/kg/infusion led to a significant decrease in SA. The three MAOi's given acutely over a range of relatively high doses had little or no effects on nicotine SA. Acute harmane caused a small, but significant, increase in nicotine SA, but only with the rats with lower than median nicotine self-administration. No impacts of acute doses of harmaline or EBC were seen. CONCLUSIONS: A non-monotonic dose-effect function of nicotine self-administration was found in female rats with higher than median baseline nicotine infusion rate, whereas rats with a lower than median rate had a monotonic function. Little or no interactive effects of MAOi's on nicotine self-administration were found.

articles.title: TIPE2/NF-κB signaling axis in osteosarcoma: mechanistic insights into its role in tumor progression.
articles.abstract: In this study, we examined the expression and cell-intrinsic function of TIPE2 in human osteosarcoma (OS). Notably, increased levels of TIPE2 expression have been observed in OS cell lines and tissues compared to normal cells and tissues, respectively. Furthermore, inhibition of TIPE2 expression through siRNA resulted in a marked reduction in the proliferative capacity, viability, and invasive characteristics of OS cells. This attenuation in OS cellular behavior was concomitant with observed alterations in autophagy-associated markers. In addition, the suppression of TIPE2 expression downregulated the expression of survivin, COX-2, cyclin A2, cyclin E, CDK-2, Runx2, MMP-9, N-cadherin, and Twist 1, while concurrently upregulated LC3B, E-cadherin, p62, p53, p21 and caspase-3. These alterations appear to be fundamentally associated with the NF-κB signaling cascade. Furthermore, our investigations revealed that the silencing of TIPE2 did not elicit significant changes in the expression levels of TNF-α, TNF-β, or TNFR1. However, it inhibited RANKL expression and NF-κB activation. Additionally, we demonstrated that silencing NF-κB does not influence TIPE2 expression, but the silencing of TNF-α and TNFR1 effectively inhibits TIPE2 expression. These observations suggest that TIPE2 operates downstream of TNF-α and TNFR1 but upstream of NF-κB. In summary, our findings identify TIPE2 as a candidate mediator of OS pathogenesis, and indicate that TIPE2 warrants further validation in vivo and in patient cohorts to establish it as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in OS.

articles.title: Targeting neuroinflammation in diabetic peripheral neuropathy: Mechanistic perspectives, phytochemical pharmacology, and translational challenges.
articles.abstract: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is a debilitating neurodegenerative complication of diabetes mellitus characterized by the convergence of metabolic dysregulation, microvascular ischemia, and chronic low-grade neuroinflammation. While intensive glycemic control and cardiometabolic risk-factor modification slow neuropathy progression-most notably in type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM)-approved central analgesic pharmacotherapies primarily manage nociceptive symptoms without directly reversing established structural axonal loss. Preclinical studies indicate that endoneurial inflammation mediated via Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), and the nucleotide-binding domain, leucine-rich-containing family, pyrin domain-containing-3 (NLRP3) inflammasome contributes to microvascular dysfunction and Schwann cell dedifferentiation. Investigational phytochemicals, including curcumin, resveratrol, berberine, and quercetin, modulate these inflammatory and oxidative nodes in experimental rodent models. However, clinical translation remains constrained by poor aqueous solubility, extensive phase II enterocytic and hepatic conjugation, active efflux, and restricted transport across the diseased blood-nerve barrier (BNB). Using a structured narrative synthesis and a three-tier evidence hierarchy, this Brief Report distinguishes established human pathogenic and clinical trial evidence from preclinical mechanistic findings, critically evaluates clinical trial limitations (sample size, duration, and subjective endpoints), and defines rigorous pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic criteria required to validate nanocarrier-mediated endoneurial target engagement.

articles.title: Integrated population pharmacokinetic modeling of endogenous baseline and exogenous choline following oral choline alfoscerate administration.
articles.abstract: Choline alfoscerate is widely used to improve neurological function; however, choline is an endogenous compound that is constitutively present in the human body. Consequently, serum choline concentrations observed after drug administration represent the combined contribution of endogenous baseline levels and exogenous drug-derived choline, posing challenges for conventional pharmacokinetic (PK) interpretation. The aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a population pharmacokinetic (Pop-PK) model that integratively describes endogenous baseline choline and exogenous choline following single oral administration of choline alfoscerate. Pop-PK analysis was conducted using data from a bioequivalence study involving 36 healthy Korean male subjects. Model development followed a stepwise approach with systematic structural comparison and covariate screening. Endogenous baseline choline concentration was explicitly incorporated as an independent model component. A one-compartment model with an additive endogenous baseline component provided an empirical description of the observed serum choline concentration-time profiles, although the fitted exogenous kinetic parameters could not be independently identified as physiological processes. Inter-individual variability was identified for Ka and baseline endogenous choline concentration (BSL), and body mass index (BMI) was retained as a covariate on BSL in the final model. Internal goodness-of-fit, visual predictive check, and bootstrap diagnostics were examined; however, broad predictive intervals, temporal residual patterns, and uncertainty in selected random-effects parameters limited conclusions regarding predictive adequacy and parameter identifiability. These findings illustrate the potential utility and limitations of a constant-baseline population pharmacokinetic formulation for describing total serum choline concentrations, while further data and model evaluation are required before extrapolation to other dosing regimens or populations.

articles.title: Real-world pharmacovigilance of thromboembolic adverse events associated with osimertinib using the Japanese adverse drug event report database.
articles.abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the disproportionality, times to onset, and outcomes of thromboembolic adverse events (AEs) associated with osimertinib using data from the Japanese Adverse Drug Event Report database (JADER), with a specific focus on real-world evidence from Japan, an East Asian country with high EGFR mutation prevalence. We analyzed JADER data from April 2004 to December 2024. Disproportionality was assessed by calculating reporting odds ratios (RORs). Time-to-onset was evaluated, and Weibull distribution parameters were calculated for major AEs with detected signals, while rare AEs were summarized descriptively. Among 3,221,393 reports, 7134 AEs were associated with osimertinib, including 153 thromboembolic AEs. Significant disproportionality signals were detected for six thromboembolic AEs: deep vein thrombosis (ROR = 2.89), pulmonary embolism (ROR = 2.78), embolism venous (ROR = 6.64), peripheral vein thrombosis (ROR = 3.16), pulmonary artery thrombosis (ROR = 2.93), and thrombophlebitis migrans (ROR = 7.49). Median onset times ranged from 28 to 85 days after osimertinib initiation. Weibull analysis of major thromboembolic AEs suggested no clear time-dependent increase in reporting frequency over time (random failure type). Fatal outcomes were observed for several thromboembolic AEs, particularly pulmonary embolism and pulmonary artery thrombosis. Several thromboembolic AEs associated with osimertinib were identified, including potentially fatal events. These findings suggest that thromboembolic events may be reported relatively early after the initiation of osimertinib treatment and highlight the importance of clinical awareness and appropriate monitoring during treatment. However, these findings do not establish a causal relationship between osimertinib and thromboembolic events.

articles.title: Protective effects of intermittent fasting and vitamin E against hyperthyroidism-associated ocular complications in Wistar rats.
articles.abstract: Our study endeavours to prevent hyperthyroidism-associated ocular complications through the synergy of intermittent fasting and vitamin E supplementation. Our aim was to reduce the incidence of hyperthyroidism-associated ocular complications by combining these two interventions, while carefully monitoring dietary intake and supplementing with vitamin E. In this experiment, animals were divided into normal, hyperthyroidism control, dual, vitamin E, and intermittent fasting groups. Hyperthyroidism was induced by administering thyroxine for 24 days. Animals in the treatment groups took vitamin E and practised intermittent fasting. Intraocular pressure was measured weekly during the protocol. After the protocol, antioxidant status, malondialdehyde and nitrite level, protein content, retinal pictures, histopathology of lens and thyroid profile were analysed. Rats with hyperthyroidism control exhibited elevated (p < 0.001) intraocular pressure, lipid peroxidation, total protein content, and thyroid hormone levels, while antioxidant and nitrite levels decreased (p < 0.001). However, our non-drug therapy significantly (p < 0.001) improved all of these parameters, bringing them to their optimum levels. Intermittent fasting prevented ocular disease caused by hyperthyroidism by reducing oxidative stress and fibro genic matter deposition, and modulating nitrite balance. It works best when combined with vitamin E for superior antioxidant benefits. Our proposed remedies not only improved ocular function but also provided physiological benefits, suggesting a link to metabolic, ophthalmic, and neurogenic diseases in future projections.

articles.title: Roxadustat for treatment of suspected erythropoietin(EPO)-induced pure red cell aplasia in a hemodialysis patient: a case report.
articles.abstract: Anemia is a prevalent complication in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly those undergoing dialysis. Recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEPO) is widely administered to patients both on and off dialysis to manage this anemia. However, despite an initial favorable therapeutic response, a sudden and unexplained decline in hemoglobin (Hb) levels often prompts the need for further diagnostic evaluation. In this context, we report a clinical case involving a 48-year-old male patient who had been undergoing hemodialysis (HD) for two years. During the course of his rhEPO treatment regimen, he may have developed pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), a rare but serious adverse reaction. Upon recognition of this complication, the administration of rhEPO was promptly discontinued, and the patient was initiated on roxadustat therapy. Following nine months of continuous roxadustat treatment, the patient experienced a significant and sustained increase in his Hb levels. This clinical outcome underscores the importance of prompt diagnosis and intervention in cases of suspected erythropoietin (EPO)-induced PRCA. Furthermore, our findings suggest that roxadustat may serve as a viable and effective therapeutic option for patients with suspected EPO-induced PRCA, potentially obviating the need for immunosuppressive therapy and its associated risks.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of adjunctive use of rifaximin in preventing radiotherapy-induced diarrhea in cancer patients: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Radiation-induced diarrhea (RID) is a common, dose-limiting toxicity in patients with pelvic cancer undergoing radiotherapy. No pharmacological agent is currently approved for its prevention. Rifaximin, a non-absorbable antibiotic with anti-inflammatory and microbiota-modulating properties, may offer protective benefits. This prospective, parallel-group, open-label randomized controlled trial enrolled 80 adults with non-metastatic pelvic cancers receiving curative-intent radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy. Participants were randomized in 1:1 ratio to receive standard care alone or standard care plus rifaximin 550 mg twice daily throughout radiotherapy. Primary outcome was the incidence of grade ≥ 2 diarrhea assessed by Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE v5.0). Secondary outcomes included time to diarrhea onset, stool consistency (Bristol scale), dehydration, quality of life assessed using European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30), and safety. Patients' follow-up lasted 3 months post-radiotherapy. Seventy-eight patients completed the study. Incidence of grade ≥ 2 diarrhea was comparable between groups (23.1% control vs. 17.9% rifaximin; risk difference [95% CI] - 5.1 [ - 23.0, 12.8]). Time to onset and rescue medication use did not differ significantly. Stool consistency and dehydration rates were comparable. Rifaximin significantly improved global health status at end of radiotherapy (mean difference between control and rifaximin groups [95% CI] - 10.5 [ - 18.5, - 2.4]) and at three months (- 7.0 [ - 13.1, - 1.0]), with lower fatigue (14.5 [4.2, 24.9]) and pain scores (12.8 [3.1, 22.5]). Adverse events were mild and comparable between groups. Adjunctive rifaximin did not reduce incidence or severity of RID but was associated with improved quality of life and symptom burden. Rifaximin was well tolerated. Larger, double-blind trials are warranted to confirm these findings and explore optimized dosing and timing of administration. Registration of the study: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06783153.

articles.title: Integrated transcriptomic and single-cell analysis identifies quercetin as a potential therapeutic candidate for osteoarthritis by targeting inflammation-related hub genes.
articles.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is closely associated with inflammatory activation, chondrocyte phenotypic alteration, and remodeling of the joint microenvironment. However, the key molecular network underlying these changes and its druggable targets remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify OA-related hub genes and explore the potential therapeutic relevance of quercetin through integrated bioinformatics and experimental validation. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between OA and control samples were screened using the GSE55235 dataset. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify phenotype-related modules. Candidate genes were obtained by intersecting DEGs, key module genes, and OA-associated genes from GeneCards. A protein-protein interaction network was constructed, followed by hub gene selection using multiple Cytoscape algorithms. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses, single-cell analysis based on GSE169454, drug prediction, and molecular docking were then performed. Finally, the effects of quercetin on hub gene expression were examined in LPS-stimulated immortalized chondrocytes. A total of 1022 DEGs were identified, and the turquoise module containing 597 genes was selected by WGCNA. Intersecting DEGs, module genes, and GeneCards-derived genes yielded 127 candidate genes. Five hub genes, namely, IL6, PTPRC, VEGFA, MYC, and NFKBIA, were further identified. Enrichment analyses linked these genes to inflammatory response, immune regulation, cell adhesion, NF-κB signaling, TNF signaling, and osteoclast differentiation. Single-cell analysis revealed heterogeneous expression of hub genes across chondrocyte subpopulations and microenvironment-related cells. Drug prediction and molecular docking suggested favorable binding between quercetin and the five hub proteins. In vitro experiments confirmed that quercetin reduced LPS-induced expression of VEGFA, PTPRC, NFKBIA, MYC, and IL-6. This study identifies five OA-related hub genes and suggests that quercetin may protect chondrocytes by modulating inflammatory and NF-κB-associated signaling.

articles.title: Brain disorders susceptibility induced by environmental pollutant lindane: possible phytotherapy amelioration by ferulic acid.
articles.abstract: Lindane (LIN) is an organochlorine pesticide with well-documented neurotoxic, genotoxic, and pro-oxidant properties. Owing to its environmental persistence and bioaccumulation, LIN can induce oxidative stress, DNA damage, apoptosis, and neuroinflammatory responses. This study aimed to investigate LIN-induced cellular toxicity and evaluate the potential protective effects of ferulic acid (FA) in C6, CTX TNA2, and RHiN neural cells. Oxidative stress parameters, including total antioxidant status (TAS), total oxidant status (TOS), and oxidative stress index (OSI), were evaluated. DNA damage was assessed using the comet assay, while apoptosis was determined using the TUNEL assay. Additionally, TLR1-10 gene and protein expression levels were analyzed to evaluate alterations in inflammatory signaling. LIN altered oxidative stress-related parameters, DNA damage, apoptotic cell death, and TLR expression across the three cell types. Notably, the oxidative stress response varied between cell lines, with OSI decreasing in LIN-treated CTX TNA2 cells. In contrast, FA treatment was associated with changes in antioxidant and oxidative stress-related parameters; however, potential interference of FA with the TAS assay should be considered when interpreting its apparent antioxidant effects. Comet and TUNEL assays further revealed treatment-related changes in DNA damage and apoptosis, while TLR expression changes varied according to cell type and treatment. LIN-induced cellular responses differed among the neural cell models examined. FA may modulate some of the effects associated with LIN exposure; however, the interpretation of TAS findings requires caution because of potential assay interference. These findings highlight the importance of considering cell-specific responses and assay-related limitations when evaluating the potential protective effects of FA against LIN-induced neural damage.

articles.title: Progression-free survival of 23 months with second-line trastuzumab deruxtecan in HER2-positive gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma: a case report.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has been approved for the second-line therapy of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive advanced gastric cancer, revolutionizing the treatment landscape for this clinical scenario. CASE PRESENTATION: Given the lack of real-world evidence, here we reported a patient with HER2-positive, metastatic gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma treated with T-DXd in the second-line setting. The patient, a 63-year-old male, previously received first-line treatment with trastuzumab plus oxaliplatin, capecitabine and sintilimab but disease progression occurred at 4.5 months. He subsequently received T-DXd-based therapy for a total of 22 treatment cycles and achieved a progression-free survival (PFS) of 23 months, with improved performance status and no T-DXd treatment dose reduction during treatment. CONCLUSION: This case firstly supplements the real-world data of T-DXd for patients with HER2-positive advanced gastric cancer in the second-line setting. These data indicate the PFS benefit with second-line T-DXd-based treatment even after rapid progression on trastuzumab-based therapy and the safety of full-dose T-DXd during long-course treatment.

articles.title: Antiplatelet Use in the Setting of Therapeutic Anticoagulation: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Patients receiving therapeutic oral anticoagulation (OAC) often have indications for antiplatelet therapy. Historically, antiplatelet agents have been used alongside therapeutic anticoagulation, increasing the risk of bleeding without a proven reduction in thrombosis. This scoping review summarizes recent evidence evaluating OAC monotherapy compared with combination therapy consisting of OAC plus antiplatelet agent among patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and prosthetic heart valves. We searched PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, and International Pharmaceutical Abstracts to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating these strategies. Included studies enrolled adults receiving therapeutic anticoagulation across different cardiovascular disease states that reported efficacy and safety outcomes. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Published subgroup analyses of included RCTs were also reviewed. After screening 10,008 records, 11 RCTs met inclusion criteria. Evidence supporting OAC monotherapy was observed in patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary artery disease; OAC monotherapy consistently reduced bleeding without increasing ischemic events compared with combination therapy. Similar reductions in bleeding were observed in patients with cerebrovascular disease, although evidence remains limited by small sample size and early trial termination. Among patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement with an indication for chronic anticoagulation, OAC monotherapy reduced bleeding without compromising ischemic outcomes. Evidence supporting discontinuation of antiplatelet therapy in patients with mechanical heart valves remains limited. Additional RCTs are needed to better define the role of antiplatelet therapy in cerebrovascular disease, prosthetic heart valves, and other high-risk populations.

articles.title: Unmasking Hidden Risks in Herbal Weight-Loss Supplements: LC-MS/MS - Based Detection of Sibutramine Adulteration for Consumer Safety Assessment.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Herbal weight-loss supplements are widely perceived as safe alternatives to synthetic drugs; however, illegal adulteration with undeclared pharmaceuticals remains a significant public health concern. Sibutramine, withdrawn from the market because of serious cardiovascular risks, is one of the most frequently detected adulterants. This study aimed to develop and validate a sensitive liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) method to detection of sibutramine in herbal dietary supplements, and to evaluate the presence of sibutramine in commercially available some of the selected products. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed sibutramine by ultra high-performance LC-MS/MS using a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer with electrospray ionization in multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) mode. Identification was based on the protonated precursor ion (m/z 280) and characteristic product-ion transitions. The method was validated for linearity, limits of detection and quantification, recovery, accuracy, precision, robustness, and matrix effects in accordance with internationally accepted bioanalytical validation guidelines. RESULTS: The method demonstrated excellent linearity over the range of 5-500 µg/L (r2 = 0.99987), with detection and quantification limits of 0.82 µg/L and 2.73 µg/L, respectively. Validation demonstrated satisfactory accuracy, precision, recovery, robustness, and negligible matrix effects, confirming the method's suitability for routine analysis. Analysis of 17 commercially available herbal weight-loss supplements revealed the presence of sibutramine in 15 samples (88%), with concentrations ranging from trace levels to substantial amounts, indicating widespread adulteration. CONCLUSION: The validated LC-MS/MS method provides a rapid, sensitive, and reliable approach for routine monitoring of sibutramine in herbal dietary supplements. The high prevalence of sibutramine detected in marketed products highlights the persistent problem of illegal adulteration and underscores the need for continuous market surveillance, stricter regulatory enforcement, and routine analytical screening to safeguard public health and ensure product quality.

articles.title: Transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGF-β1) putatively modulates central noradrenergic neurotransmission via a TGF-β receptor type 1 (TGF-βR1)-mediated mechanism in male rats.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) signaling has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, but its direct electrophysiological effects on central monoaminergic neurons remain unclear. This study examined whether TGF-β1 modulates serotonergic, dopaminergic, and noradrenergic neuronal activity in vivo. METHODS: Adult male rats received acute TGF-β1 administration, and extracellular single-unit recordings were performed from serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), and noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC). Additional experiments assessed the involvement of noradrenergic neurotransmission using fusaric acid-induced noradrenaline depletion and the role of TGF-β receptor type I (TGF-βR1) using the antagonist LY2109761. RESULTS: TGF-β1 did not significantly alter the firing activity of DRN serotonergic neurons or VTA dopaminergic neurons. In contrast, TGF-β1 significantly reduced the spontaneous firing activity and burst parameters of LC noradrenergic neurons. Noradrenaline depletion with fusaric acid abolished the inhibitory effect of TGF-β1 on LC neuronal activity. Conversely, pharmacological blockade of TGF-βR1 with LY2109761 increased LC neuronal firing, suggesting that endogenous TGF-β1 signaling exerts a tonic inhibitory influence on the noradrenergic system. CONCLUSION: These findings identify TGF-β1/TGF-βR1 signaling as a selective modulator of central noradrenergic neuronal activity. The apparent involvement of noradrenergic signaling in the suppression of LC firing may represent a mechanism linking TGF-β1 signaling with monoaminergic circuits involved in stress regulation and affective disorders.

articles.title: Editorial: 4Rs in ethnopharmacology - reduce, refine, replace and responsibility using animal models.
Effects of Agomelatine on Sleep Quality, Anxiety, Depression, Appetite, and Fatigue During Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation: A Triple-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, reduced appetite, and fatigue are common among patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and can adversely affect quality of life and recovery. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of agomelatine on sleep quality, anxiety, depression, appetite, and fatigue in patients undergoing HSCT. METHODS: In this clinical trial, 165 candidates were screened, and 90 patients undergoing HSCT were randomly assigned using block randomization to receive agomelatine 25 mg nightly or a matching placebo throughout hospitalization, which lasted approximately 1 month. Outcomes were assessed at admission, during the neutropenic phase, and at discharge using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Brief Fatigue Inventory, and Council on Nutrition Appetite Questionnaire. Analyses were performed using STATA version 17, with a significance threshold of P < 0.05. RESULTS: Crude group comparisons showed favorable trends in global PSQI score and its components, anxiety, depression, and appetite with agomelatine relative to placebo; most differences were not statistically significant. Fatigue showed no significant overall between-group benefit, although scores changed over time. Group-by-time interactions were statistically significant. Mean changes in PSQI component scores were lower with agomelatine across the 3 assessment periods. In particular, the mean change in the PSQI sleep-medication component score was approximately 0.5 units lower with agomelatine than with placebo (β = -0.49; 95% CI, -0.90 to -0.09; P = 0.016). No statistically significant between-group difference in reported adverse events was observed. CONCLUSIONS: Agomelatine may have a supportive role during HSCT, particularly in relation to a lower PSQI sleep-medication component score. The negative crude coefficient for the global PSQI score also favored agomelatine, although this comparison was not statistically significant. Reported adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. Larger trials, including trials evaluating a higher dose, are required to confirm treatment effects on sleep and psychological outcomes.

articles.title: Dexmedetomidine Dosing Evaluation for Sedation in Neonates Undergoing Therapeutic Hypothermia.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Recently, dexmedetomidine has replaced opioids for sedation in neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) patients with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). The study objectives were to describe dosing patterns, evaluate compliance, and compare effectiveness and safety between the original (pre-implementation) and revised (post-implementation) in-house dexmedetomidine dosing guidelines. STUDY DESIGN: This was a retrospective cohort study that included neonates with HIE admitted to a level IV NICU for therapeutic hypothermia comparing two dexmedetomidine dosing regimens: (1) pre-implementation: starting dose of 0.05 μg/kg/h followed by titration by 0.05 μg/kg/h every 6 h as needed, and (2) post-implementation: 0.2 μg/kg/h followed by titration by 0.1 μg/kg/h every 30-60 min as needed. RESULTS: A total of 106 neonates were included: 50 in the pre-implementation group and 56 in the post-implementation group. Compliance to post-implementation formulary recommendations was 69.6% for initial doses, 62.5% for dose increases, and 44.6% for dose decreases. An increased odds of opioid exposure (adjusted odds ratio: 7.13, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.59-51.5, p = 0.02) and greater proportion of bradycardia (21.4% vs. 4%, p = 0.03) were observed in the post-implementation group. No significant differences in effectiveness end points or hypotension were observed between groups (p ≥ 0.05). CONCLUSION: Compliance with formulary-recommended dexmedetomidine dosing was variable and dose decreases were common in the post-implementation group. The post-implementation dosing approach was not associated with improved effectiveness outcomes (sedation) but was associated with greater opioid exposure and more bradycardia, supporting the need for further prospective evaluation to determine the optimal dexmedetomidine dosing in neonates undergoing HIE.

articles.title: Retraction Note: Resveratrol promotes liver cell survival in mice liver-induced ischemia-reperfusion through unfolded protein response: a possible approach in liver transplantation.
Rethinking Micro/Nanoplastics Neurotoxicity: Current Challenges and Future Directions.
articles.abstract: Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) are increasingly recognized as potential neurotoxicants, yet the extent to which experimental evidence translates into human neurological risk remains uncertain. Human studies have reported MNP-associated signals in central nervous system (CNS)-related samples, and experimental models have shown neurological and neurobehavioral effects. Detection alone does not establish neurotoxicity, and extrapolation of experimental findings to humans requires consideration of particle characteristics, exposure patterns, and biological susceptibility. A critical challenge is therefore to determine whether observed neurotoxic effects occur under environmentally and human-relevant conditions and whether brain-associated MNP burdens are causally linked to adverse neurological outcomes. Here, we critically examine current challenges in MNP neurotoxicity research, with particular emphasis on exposure realism, dose interpretation, measurement standardization, model relevance, mechanistic interpretation, and translation to human health. To address these limitations, we propose an exposure-measurement-model-mechanism-translation (EMMMT) framework that integrates environmentally realistic exposure systems, standardized and reproducible MNP characterization and measurement, complementary human and animal CNS models, integrated mechanistic investigations, and adverse outcome pathway (AOP)-oriented translation. This framework provides a structured roadmap for moving the field beyond proof-of-presence toward causal, reproducible, and human-relevant evidence of neurotoxicity. Ultimately, strengthening the linkage between MNP exposure, brain burden, cellular dose, molecular and cellular perturbations, and adverse neurological outcomes will be essential for advancing evidence-based human health risk assessment.

articles.title: Selexipag as a Therapeutic Alternative for Treprostinil-Induced Thrombocytopenia in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Parenteral prostacyclin pathway agent-induced thrombocytopenia may require dose reduction or therapy discontinuation to mitigate the adverse events. However, the pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) guidelines do not suggest any strategy to overcome treprostinil-induced thrombocytopenia. Selexipag is an oral, non-prostanoid, selective IP receptor agonist. This is the first case report proposing the use of selexipag, due to its minimal thrombocytopenia risk, when severe treprostinil-induced thrombocytopenia occurs in practice. A 66-year-old woman presented to the hospital with new-onset PAH and right ventricular dysfunction. Due to the high mortality risk, the patient was initially started on intravenous treprostinil. The clinical course was complicated by probable treprostinil-induced thrombocytopenia. Due to the need for prostacyclin pathway therapy, the decision was made to switch from intravenous treprostinil to oral selexipag. The nadir platelet count was 30,000/μL. Approximately 72 h after discontinuation of treprostinil and maintaining selexipag 1600 mcg twice daily, the platelet count improved to 46,000/μL on the day of discharge. Several days after discharge, the platelet count further improved to 55,000/μL. The repeated platelet count 1 month after discharge normalized to 329,000/μL. Our case report described the successful use of selexipag to overcome treprostinil-induced thrombocytopenia, owing to its limited effect on platelet aggregation.
